From Seeing to Reporting: A Theory of Reliable
Visual Set Generation in Vision-Language Models

Junzhe Shi ††thanks: Corresponding author: Junzhe Shi. Affiliation: Systems Engineering Affiliation: University of California, Berkeley Affiliation: Berkeley, CA, USA Email: junzhe@berkeley.edu    Yuan Gan Affiliation: Department of AI Affiliation: Quotr AI Affiliation: Emeryville, CA, USA Email: yuan@quotr.ai    Shida Jiang Affiliation: Systems Engineering Affiliation: University of California, Berkeley Affiliation: Berkeley, CA, USA Email: shida_jiang@berkeley.edu
Abstract

Vision-language models (VLMs) are asked to report what they see: to count objects, box them, parse a screen or pick a click target (GUI grounding). We argue that reporting is part of the visual task, not merely its formatting. In a dense scene with 173 shapes, GPT-6.1 lists 173 records that match every shape, yet the counts it states in the same response sum to 188. From Seeing to Reporting (FSR) is a theory of visual reporting and a set of inference-time procedures that improve the reports of frozen VLMs. It models reporting as a chain from responses to decoded records, constructed sets and task answers, linked by task-compatible matching. The chain gives exact relations for deleting records, averaging their coordinates and switching readouts, and it splits the error of one answer chosen among several calls into missing candidates, lost representatives and wrong choices. These relations guide procedures for counting, detection, document layout, screen parsing and GUI grounding that use the task specification and a shipped configuration, without requiring labels from the target task. On 50 dense synthetic scenes, a one-call reporting-and-decoding protocol cuts per-type count error by 85.2% for GPT-6.1 and 98.8% for Claude Sonnet 5.5. On 600 ScreenSpot-Pro items, a GUI-grounding tier that combines three models lowers the miss rate from 13.67% for GPT-6.1’s two-stage zoom to 9.33%, against 12.67% for three such zooms combined by a cluster vote at about the same cost. A plain vote over the same three models misses 12.33%: the other models supply the candidates, and selecting among them turns those candidates into fewer misses. We release the protocols, the stored responses and the analysis code.

1 Introduction

Vision-language models are now asked to report a set of objects in an image: to count them, to box them, to parse every element of a screen, or to pick the one element a user means (GUI grounding: given a screenshot and an instruction, return the point to click). A typical answer has two parts. The first is a list: one entry per object, each giving a class name and a location (a point or a box). We call each entry a record. The second, when it is requested, is a stated count: the numbers the model writes for how many objects of each class it found. Code can also count the records in the list; we call that the list count. The two counts should agree. Often they do not.

Figure 1a shows one response of GPT-6.1 to a dense synthetic scene with 173 shapes of five classes. Its list has 173 records, and each record matches a different shape of the same class within 20 pixels, so the list is exact. In the same response, the model states counts that add up to 188. Across 50 such scenes, GPT-6.1 wrote an exact list in 20 scenes, and in 19 of them its stated counts were wrong. Sonnet 5.5 wrote an exact list in 39 scenes (after mapping its word “diamond” to the class “square”), and its stated counts were wrong in all 39. The response contains a correct enumeration; the model’s own summary of that enumeration is not faithful to it.

Visual set reports are becoming the interface between perception models and the systems that use them: inventory counts, document layout, screen parsing for computer-use agents, click targets. Practitioners compensate with folklore: ask again, ask the model to check itself, overlay a grid, tell it not to miss anything, vote across models. Some of these help, some do nothing, and some make things worse. Without a model of where reporting errors come from, it is hard to predict which. Our thesis is that reporting is part of the visual task, not merely its formatting: what a model delivers depends on how it is asked to report, how the report is decoded and read, and how several reports are combined, and each of these steps can be analysed and improved.

What we do.

We describe reporting as a chain with four objects (Figure 2): a response, the raw text of one call to a model; the records decoded from it; a set of records built from one or more responses, for example by keeping only records that two calls agree on; and the task answer read from that set, such as a count per class or a click point. Three quantities connect the chain to every loss we study: the maximum number of records that can be paired one-to-one with true objects under the task’s matching rule, the number of records that are scored, and the rule that reads the answer. They give exact relations for what each operation does. Deleting unconfirmed records lowers the error exactly when the deletion loses fewer than one match per two scored records removed (with equal costs of the two error types), whichever model or view supplied the confirmation. Averaging the coordinates of agreeing records is a separate effect that can help or hurt. The chain takes reports as they come: from one call on the whole image, or from several views produced by an existing view planner such as tiling or zoom, whose merging and cross-view confirmation are constructions like any other. Alongside these relations we state a behavioural model, kept separate from them: each object has a persistent tendency to be reported or missed, partly shared across models. This analysis of what a model reports complements analyses of what a single call can see (Shi et al., 2026).

Seeing and reporting.

The title names the two things the chain separates. What a set of calls has seen is its coverage: the correct records or candidates present anywhere in the responses, in any field, view or model. What is reported is a selection from that coverage: which field is read, which records are kept, which point is output. The repairs in this paper add coverage, improve the selection, or, by averaging coordinates, move the records that are kept; on a fixed set of calls an operation helps exactly when, on what it changes, the errors it repairs outweigh the correct outputs it breaks, at the exchange rate the loss sets (Section 4). Reading the list instead of the stated count, and deleting unconfirmed records, change only the selection. A smaller view or a second model adds coverage, and a selection must then use it: on 600 click items, three models’ points with a plain vote have a miss rate not significantly different from that of three calls of one model, and choosing among the same points with a scorer and a comparison removes 18 more misses. Detecting and judging ask what the outputs alone reveal about a selection.

Three problems, kept apart.

Practice often treats three problems as one. Detecting that a report is wrong can be done without labels, from disagreement between reports (Proposition 6). Judging which of several reports or configurations is more accurate cannot in general be certified from outputs alone, because two scenes can produce the same outputs (Proposition 11); it needs labels, on the task itself or on related sources from which a configuration is carried over (Section 7.9). Repairing a report works when the needed information is already available: in another field of the same response, in another view of the image, or in another model’s report. A method that detects errors well need not judge well, and one that judges well need not repair. A model asked at run time to score or compare candidate answers, as in our GUI-grounding tier, is one more source of evidence for a repair, not a certificate. The paper is organized around this distinction.

Three answers. Do vision-language models report what they see? Not reliably, and the gap is visible within one response: in dense scenes GPT-6.1 and Sonnet 5.5 often write an exact list while the counts they state in the same response are wrong. Will better models make the repairs unnecessary? Some failures are already absent on our tasks: on our synthetic counting scenes, the average coordinate offset is about 1% of the matching tolerance, and Gemini 3.8’s default reasoning setting removes most of its broken lists. The gap between list and stated count, and object-level errors that repeat across calls, remain in the newest models we tested. More calls of the same model, or a different source of evidence? For counts, clicks and error detection, a different source helped more: another field of the same response, the original pixels of a smaller crop, or a different model. Repeating the same call helps mainly by removing false records that do not repeat.

What we find.

Measured against common remedies on the same stored calls (Section 7.1) and, for clicks, on 600 further items (Section 7.7), the shipped defaults do better than these remedies in most comparisons, and the theory’s quantities say where and why.

  • •

    Repair the readout. On dense synthetic scenes with five classes, counting the list instead of reading the stated count cuts per-type count error by 71% to 84% in the same responses of GPT-6.1 and Sonnet 5.5, and the full list-first protocol cuts it by 85.2% and 98.8% at the cost of one call, where self-consistency over three calls gains at most 23%. On one-class photographs, and on aerial and document images where the lists themselves miss objects, the protocol’s change is small and not significant for these two models; Gemini 3.8 needs its default setting, at which far fewer of its lists break (flagged lists 90% to 12%) (Sections 7.2 and 7.3).

  • •

    Repair the set. When a partner call confirms the records of a base call, the change in set error splits exactly into deleting the records the partner does not report and averaging the coordinates of those it does. Deletion helps when the marginal matching rate p1p_{1} of the deleted records is below 1/21/2; the task family’s default decides correctly in 85% of draws over 54 base/partner pairs, and five labelled images cut the loss from a wrong decision from 0.43 to 0.17 errors per image. Confirmation is a default for set error on over-reporting families only; for F1 the default is a single call (Sections 7.4 and 7.9).

  • •

    Repair the view. Two-stage zoom cuts the miss rate by 65% for Gemini 3.8 and 41% for Sonnet 5.5 (not significant for GPT-6.1), where a three-click vote or zooming only on disagreement gains at most 13%. Confirming a whole-image report with four crop reports cuts set error by up to 45.5% and hurts where p1>1/2p_{1}>1/2 (Section 7.5).

  • •

    Detect. A second, cheaper model catches 61% of GPT-6.1’s misses and a second call of the same model 17%, at the price of flagging more items (Section 7.6).

  • •

    Repair a click by choosing among models. The miss rate of one answer chosen among several calls splits exactly into three terms: no correct candidate, no correct cluster representative, a wrong choice among representatives. FSR’s GUI-grounding tier, built on this split, misses 9.33% of 600 ScreenSpot-Pro targets, against 13.67% for GPT-6.1’s two-stage zoom, 12.67% for three such zooms at about the same cost, and 12.33% for a plain vote over the same three models’ points; against a crop-first baseline the difference, −2.17-2.17 points, has an interval that reaches zero (Section 7.7).

  • •

    Judge. With the truth, choosing the best set among three calls of one model would remove 45% of set error; selectors fitted with labels reach 16%. Defaults chosen on other sources transfer: three-call unanimity improves set error significantly in 9 of 15 over-reporting cells and significantly worsens none, and a single-call configuration chosen on three detection sources raises macro F1 on the fourth from 42.1 to 49.1 (Sections 7.8 and 7.9).

Contributions.

Our contribution is a common task-loss model for visual reporting, procedures that act on its stages, and experiments that separate what information is available from the quality of the answer finally delivered. The model covers multi-record outputs and the single-record case of click grounding. Its exact relations do not prescribe one universal interface; they say what each operation can change and what must be measured to decide whether the change is useful.

  1. 1.

    A common theory of reporting operations and task quality. A chain from response to records, set and answer, in which task-compatible matching, scored record counts and the readout express the losses for counts, boxes, screen elements and clicks; exact relations for deletion, coordinate averaging and readout; conditions, stated as inequalities on confirmation rates, under which repetition, a new view or a second model helps, with a behavioural model of persistent errors; a constrained oracle for any declared family of candidate sets; an exact split of the error of one answer chosen among several calls, with the effect of adding a source and of switching an answer; and an impossibility result for certifying a report from outputs alone (Sections 3 and 4).

  2. 2.

    Executable procedures for recovering, constructing and selecting visual records. A default pipeline that dispatches by task and budget, and a several-model GUI-grounding tier, in which every input is named (task specification, shipped configuration, computed from the outputs, or optional labels), together with the revisions of the model that led to them (Section 5).

  3. 3.

    Mechanism-resolving evidence and a fixed-protocol evaluation of complete task outputs. Measurements on 67,364 calls to five proprietary models and one open-weight model that attribute gains and failures to single operations, and a 600-item click evaluation of the complete tier. All responses, the labels whose licences allow redistribution, a script that rebuilds the others from the official downloads, and the code that regenerates every table and figure are at https://github.com/shijunzhe/vlm-set-reporting (Sections 6 and 7).

2 Related Work

Counting and set reporting by VLMs.

Counting is a long-standing weak spot of vision-language models (Paiss et al., 2023; Rahmanzadehgervi et al., 2024), and recent work locates part of the failure after perception: count information can be present in internal representations yet misaligned with the emitted number (El-Shangiti et al., 2026), and a visual counting bottleneck has been isolated in the model pipeline (Pang et al., 2026). Training-free fixes divide the image and count per region (Qharabagh et al., 2026), in the spirit of sliced inference for small-object detection (Akyon et al., 2022). Point-and-count supervision (Deitke et al., 2025) and sequence-style detection (Chen et al., 2022; Li et al., 2025a) make the list itself the output. Program-based visual reasoning counts by running code over the items a model finds (Gupta and Kembhavi, 2023; Surís et al., 2023); we show that the same code readout repairs the counts a single model writes about its own list. We work with frozen API models and observe the same gap from the outside: the information is in the model’s own list in the same response, so the fix is a readout rule rather than a probe or a training signal. We also extend the analysis from counts to boxes, screen elements and clicks, where the loss is a matching between sets.

Views: zoom, tiles and resolution.

Zooming in improves fine-grained perception (Wu and Xie, 2024; Shen et al., 2024; Zhang et al., 2025) and GUI grounding (Jiang et al., 2025; Tang et al., 2026), and region-level consistency can be used at test time (Du et al., 2026). GUI-Lens lets a single general-purpose model crop from coarse to fine, with OCR and detector anchors and a verification step (Fu et al., 2026); Section 7.7 compares our GUI-grounding tier with a simplified crop-first baseline in its style and shows that the two err on different items. A companion study analyses when zooming in is safe for small objects (Shi et al., 2026). Uncertainty-driven zoom on open 7B models found that zooming every item can hurt (Tang et al., 2026); on frontier API models we find two-stage zoom on every item, in the style of ReGround (Li et al., 2025b), not significantly different (GPT-6.1) or better (Sonnet 5.5, Gemini 3.8), and cheaper than zooming only on disagreement. The two observations are compatible: whether zoom hurts depends on whether the crop cuts the target and on the relative cost of the second call (Section 7.5).

Visual scaffolds.

Overlaid marks and coordinate grids are a popular way to help models localize (Yang et al., 2023; Lei et al., 2025). An overlay adds no Shannon information to the sent image and can only change how the model uses it (Shi et al., 2026); we observe two such changes in current models (fewer omitted class fields for Gemini 3.8, more uses of a class name outside the vocabulary for Sonnet 5.5) and no coordinate correction, because on synthetic counting scenes their systematic coordinate offset is about 1% of the matching tolerance.

Self-consistency, self-correction and cross-model agreement.

Sampling several answers and voting improves reasoning (Wang et al., 2023), but models often fail to correct themselves (Huang et al., 2024; Madaan et al., 2023; Liao et al., 2025), and their errors can be self-consistent and hard to detect (Tan et al., 2025; Bhat and Yamasaki, 2026). Disagreement between different models complements self-consistency for uncertainty estimation (Hamidieh et al., 2026), and multi-VLM agreement has been used to verify OCR (Zhang et al., 2026); we use disagreement among three frontier models’ clicks as an alarm and choose among their points with a scoring model (Section 5.1); test-time scaling can also separate perception from reasoning (Avogaro et al., 2026). In set tasks these effects have a precise form: confirmation changes the set error by an exact identity, and whether a partner helps depends on its confirmation rates for the base model’s true and false records, not on its overall quality (Proposition 5).

Ensembles, fusion and selective prediction.

Weighted box fusion averages coordinates of matched detections (Solovyev et al., 2021), and detection ensembles combine models by affirmative, consensus or unanimous voting (Casado-García and Heras, 2020); our three-call unanimity is the unanimous strategy applied to repeated calls, and we show that its effect splits into a selection term and an averaging term, the latter of either sign under threshold matching. Error decompositions for detection split error into classification, localization, duplicate and background parts (Bolya et al., 2020; Oksuz et al., 2018); our split is instead by operation, so that each term belongs to one decision. Classical models for aggregating judges assume errors that are independent given the truth (Dawid and Skene, 1979; Grofman et al., 1983), which object-level persistence violates. Work on ensemble diversity measures how correlated the members’ errors are (Kuncheva and Whitaker, 2003), and deep ensembles obtain diversity by training members independently (Lakshminarayanan et al., 2017); our members are repeated calls of fixed models, and we measure how strongly their errors on the same object are shared. Our alarms are evaluated as risk-coverage curves, as in selective classification (Geifman and El-Yaniv, 2017). The matroid structure of matching rank (Edmonds and Fulkerson, 1965) and the assignment algorithm (Kuhn, 1955) underlie our identities and oracle, and one-to-one matching between predicted and true sets is also the loss of set-prediction detectors (Carion et al., 2020).

What is known and what is new in the theory.

Several of our relations specialise known results to record sets. The deletion threshold is the cost-sensitive decision threshold (Elkan, 2001); its F1 form matches the result that the F1-optimal threshold is half the optimal F1 (Lipton et al., 2014); diminishing coverage is the submodularity of coverage (Nemhauser et al., 1978); the certification bound is a two-point argument (Tsybakov, 2009); and the propensity model is related to labeler-expertise models (Whitehill et al., 2009). The three propositions on choosing one answer among several calls are elementary: a partition of the miss event, the chain rule, and the law of total probability. The quantity FF is the miss counterpart of pass@kk-style coverage of a candidate set; what the propositions add is the bookkeeping with representatives fixed before any choice, which makes the three terms measurable on stored calls (Section 7.7). The set-reporting setting adds three things. First, a deleted record can lose fewer matches than it held, because a remaining record may take over its target, so the threshold concerns the marginal matching rate p1p_{1} rather than precision, and p1p_{1} estimated on five labelled images, with the task family’s default as the starting point, predicts the effect of deletion on other images. Second, a selector and an oracle can be compared fairly only within the same feasible family, which the constrained oracle provides. Third, a view can confirm or reject only the records it contains, which restricts cross-view confirmation to each view’s field. The chain itself is the unifying contribution: the same three quantities, matching size, scored record count and readout, carry these results across counts, boxes, screen elements and clicks.

Benchmarks.

We use SKU-110K (Goldman et al., 2019), DOTA (Xia et al., 2018), DocLayNet (Pfitzmann et al., 2022), FSC-147 (Ranjan et al., 2021), PixMo-Count (Deitke et al., 2025), ScreenSpot-Pro (Li et al., 2025b), ScreenSpot-v2 (a corrected release of ScreenSpot; Cheng et al., 2024), GroundCUA (Feizi et al., 2026) and ScreenParse (Gurbuz et al., 2026), together with a synthetic counting probe whose labels are exact.

3.1 Terms

Table 1 defines the words used throughout the paper in plain language; the formal objects follow.

3.4 Records, clusters and feasible sets

Calls 1,…,K1,\dots,K give delivered collections Z1,…,ZKZ_{1},\dots,Z_{K}. A label-free correspondence merges them into clusters 𝒬={Q1,…}\mathcal{Q}=\{Q_{1},\dots\}: it first maximizes the number of associated pairs under the association rule of Table 2, then their overlap, against cluster representatives. A cluster has a support set sup⁡(Q)⊆{1,…,K}\mathrm{sup}(Q)\subseteq\{1,\dots,K\} (the calls that reported it), member records, and an averaged record z¯Q\bar{z}_{Q} (the coordinate mean of its members, with the class of the first member). A construction chooses, for each cluster, either nothing or one representative from a declared candidate set A⁡(Q)A(Q), so its feasible family is

𝒮A={⋃QsQ:sQ∈{∅}∪{{a}:a∈A⁡(Q)}}.\mathcal{S}_{A}=\big\{\textstyle\bigcup_{Q}s_{Q}:\ s_{Q}\in\{\varnothing\}\cup\{\{a\}:a\in A(Q)\}\big\}.

Support-kk rules use A⁡(Q)={z¯Q}A(Q)=\{\bar{z}_{Q}\} and keep QQ iff |sup⁡(Q)|≥k|\mathrm{sup}(Q)|\geq k. Deletion-only intersection uses the base call’s own record. A record gate uses A⁡(Q)={z¯Q}∪members⁡(Q)A(Q)=\{\bar{z}_{Q}\}\cup\mathrm{members}(Q). All oracles and fitted selectors compared with a construction use the same 𝒮A\mathcal{S}_{A}.

3.5 Output contract and status

The decoder reports four status layers for every call. They are distinct, and passing a lower layer never implies a higher one. L1 transport: the call returned, and its finish reason (stop, length) is recorded. L2 outer syntax: the whole response parses as the requested JSON object after stripping a code fence. L3 record validity: which records were recovered (strict parse, or a declared salvage of individual objects when the whole response does not parse), which of them are valid under the task contract, and four list-level degeneracy flags (Section 5). L4 task completeness: whether SS contains every target. L1 to L3 are checked by code; L4 cannot in general be checked without labels (Section 4.5). The procedures return SS, y^\hat{y} and σ\sigma for every input, never drop a call from cost or denominator accounting, and report the strict-JSON failure rate, so the share of salvaged responses is visible.

3.6 Losses

For a scored collection SS, let r⁡(S)r(S) be the matching size: the largest number of disjoint pairs (z,y)(z,y) with ρτ​(z,y)=1\rho_{\tau}(z,y)=1. Let c⁡(S)c(S) be the number of scored records: those matched in the maximum matching chosen by the evaluation code or lying outside Ωτ\Omega_{\tau}. Without an ignore region, c⁡(S)=|S|c(S)=|S|. With one, cc can depend on which maximum matching is chosen; the relations below hold for any fixed choice applied consistently, since they are computed from the same cc and rr. Ignore regions occur in 34 of 240 detection items and in no screen item. The set losses are functions of rr, cc and nn; the count losses also depend on the readout. With costs cFP,cFN>0c_{\mathrm{FP}},c_{\mathrm{FN}}>0,

Ew​(S)\displaystyle E_{w}(S) =cFP​[c⁡(S)−r⁡(S)]+cFN​[n−r⁡(S)],\displaystyle=c_{\mathrm{FP}}[c(S)-r(S)]+c_{\mathrm{FN}}[n-r(S)],
F1⁡(S)\displaystyle\mathrm{F1}(S) =2​r​(S)/(n+c⁡(S)),\displaystyle=2\,r(S)/(n+c(S)),

with F1=1\mathrm{F1}=1 when n=c⁡(S)=0n=c(S)=0. EE denotes EwE_{w} with cFP=cFN=1c_{\mathrm{FP}}=c_{\mathrm{FN}}=1; recall is r⁡(S)/nr(S)/n. F1 in our tables is the mean of per-image F1. The per-type count error of a readout y^\hat{y} is ∑c|y^c−nc|\sum_{c}|\hat{y}_{c}-n_{c}|, and the click loss is 1−𝟙[p^∈box(y)]1-\mathbb{1}[\hat{p}\in\mathrm{box}(y)]. Every reported number names the number of calls KK, the interface, the setting, and the loss.

4 Theory

One principle runs through the results on operations. A library of calls fixes what can be reported, its coverage; a rule applied to the library decides what is reported, its selection. On a fixed library, an operation lowers the loss exactly when, on the records or items it changes, the errors it repairs outweigh the correct outputs it breaks, at the exchange rate the loss sets. Section 4.1 states the exact relations for record sets: deleting records, averaging their coordinates, and reading a different field of one response. Section 4.2 gives a behavioural model of how models report objects across repeated calls, views and models, which says when a partner adds coverage; unlike the relations, it is an assumption to be checked. Section 4.3 bounds what selection over a fixed library can reach. Section 4.4 treats a single answer chosen among several calls: the three places where a miss can arise, the coverage an added source brings, and the net effect of switching an answer, which is the principle’s form for clicks. Section 4.5 states what outputs alone cannot certify. Table 3 lists, for each result the method uses, the quantity it measures, the decision it makes and where it is checked. Proofs and supporting results are in Appendix A.

4.1 Exact relations between operations and losses

Proposition 1 (Deletion and addition).

Let S⊆AS\subseteq A, let Δ​c=c⁡(A)−c⁡(S)\Delta c=c(A)-c(S) be the net decrease in scored records and Δ​r=r⁡(A)−r⁡(S)\Delta r=r(A)-r(S) the number of matches lost. Then exactly

Ew​(A)−Ew​(S)=cFP​Δ​c−(cFP+cFN)​Δ​r,E_{w}(A)-E_{w}(S)=c_{\mathrm{FP}}\,\Delta c-(c_{\mathrm{FP}}+c_{\mathrm{FN}})\,\Delta r,

and in particular E⁡(A)−E⁡(S)=Δ​c−2​Δ​rE(A)-E(S)=\Delta c-2\Delta r. Addition is the same relation read in reverse.

Proposition 2 (Intersection threshold).

Deleting A∖SA\setminus S lowers weighted set error if and only if cFP​Δ​c>(cFP+cFN)​Δ​rc_{\mathrm{FP}}\,\Delta c>(c_{\mathrm{FP}}+c_{\mathrm{FN}})\,\Delta r, that is, for Δ​c>0\Delta c>0, iff Δ​r/Δ​c<cFP/(cFP+cFN)\Delta r/\Delta c<c_{\mathrm{FP}}/(c_{\mathrm{FP}}+c_{\mathrm{FN}}). Adding a non-empty set lowers weighted set error iff (cFP+cFN)(c_{\mathrm{FP}}+c_{\mathrm{FN}}) times the matches gained exceeds cFPc_{\mathrm{FP}} times the scored records added.

In words: deleting records helps when few enough of them were matched. Over a population of images with 𝔼⁡[Δ​c]>0\mathbb{E}[\Delta c]>0, the expected change has the sign of cFP/(cFP+cFN)−p1c_{\mathrm{FP}}/(c_{\mathrm{FP}}+c_{\mathrm{FN}})-p_{1}, where p1:=𝔼⁡[Δ​r]/𝔼⁡[Δ​c]p_{1}:=\mathbb{E}[\Delta r]/\mathbb{E}[\Delta c] is the ratio of expected matches lost to expected records removed. We call p1p_{1} the marginal matching rate of the deleted records; it is not the average of per-image precisions, and it equals the precision of the deleted records only when no remaining record can take over a deleted record’s match. For EE the threshold is 1/21/2. This is the cost-sensitive decision threshold (Elkan, 2001) applied to the records a partner does not confirm; what is specific to record sets is that Δ​r\Delta r can be smaller than the number of matched records deleted, so the relevant rate is p1p_{1} and not their precision. The proposition does not assume that the confirming report comes from the same model, the same view, or any probability model. It concerns deletion only: the retained records keep their coordinates.

For F1 the same argument gives a per-image threshold of F1⁡(A)/2\mathrm{F1}(A)/2 in place of 1/21/2 (Corollary 2 in Appendix A), the marginal form of the known result that the F1-optimal threshold of a calibrated classifier is half its optimal F1 (Lipton et al., 2014). Because F1⁡(A)/2≤1/2\mathrm{F1}(A)/2\leq 1/2, a deletion that raises F1 on an image also lowers EE there, but not conversely. This agrees with the defaults of Section 7.9: confirmation for set error on over-reporting sources, a single call for F1. In the deletion case, the threshold is the same exchange rate as the price of a false output in the companion analysis of decomposition (Shi et al., 2026).

Proposition 3 (Geometry term).

Let S0⊆AS_{0}\subseteq A be the confirmed records with their original coordinates and SfS_{f} the same clusters with averaged coordinates. Then

E⁡(A)−E⁡(Sf)=\displaystyle E(A)-E(S_{f})=\ [E⁡(A)−E⁡(S0)]⏟selection (Prop. 1)\displaystyle\underbrace{[E(A)-E(S_{0})]}_{\text{selection (Prop.~\ref{prop:identity})}}
+[E⁡(S0)−E⁡(Sf)]⏟geometry,\displaystyle+\underbrace{[E(S_{0})-E(S_{f})]}_{\text{geometry}},

and the geometry term equals [c⁡(S0)−c⁡(Sf)]−2​[r⁡(S0)−r⁡(Sf)][c(S_{0})-c(S_{f})]-2[r(S_{0})-r(S_{f})].

By convexity, the mean of a cluster’s members is no farther, in mean squared distance, from any fixed target than the members are on average. That does not make every averaged record closer than its best member, and matching uses a threshold, so the geometry term can have either sign. On DocLayNet with GPT-6.1 confirmed by Sonnet 5.5 (60 images), E⁡(A)=8.567E(A)=8.567, E⁡(S0)=7.767E(S_{0})=7.767 and E⁡(Sf)=8.867E(S_{f})=8.867: selection gains 0.8000.800, geometry loses 1.1001.100, and the intersection with averaged coordinates is worse than the single call although deletion alone is better.

Proposition 4 (Two readouts of one response).

Let a decoded response have delivered records ZZ and stated counts d≠∅d\neq\varnothing, and let lc​(Z)c=#⁡{z∈Z:class⁡(z)=c}\mathrm{lc}(Z)_{c}=\#\{z\in Z:\mathrm{class}(z)=c\} be the list count. Both readouts come from the same response, so the difference between their errors ‖d−n‖1\|d-n\|_{1} and ‖lc⁡(Z)−n‖1\|\mathrm{lc}(Z)-n\|_{1} isolates the readout and holds generation fixed. The gap ‖d−lc⁡(Z)‖1\|d-\mathrm{lc}(Z)\|_{1} is observable without labels, and

max⁡{‖d−n‖1,‖lc⁡(Z)−n‖1}≥12​‖d−lc⁡(Z)‖1,\max\{\|d-n\|_{1},\|\mathrm{lc}(Z)-n\|_{1}\}\ \geq\ \tfrac{1}{2}\|d-\mathrm{lc}(Z)\|_{1},
|‖d−n‖1−‖lc⁡(Z)−n‖1|≤‖d−lc⁡(Z)‖1.\big|\,\|d-n\|_{1}-\|\mathrm{lc}(Z)-n\|_{1}\big|\ \leq\ \|d-\mathrm{lc}(Z)\|_{1}.

A positive gap shows that at least one readout is wrong; it does not show which. A small gap shows that no choice between the two readouts can change the error by more than the gap, whatever the truth: choosing a readout can never gain more than the gap, and errors that both readouts share, such as objects missing from the list and from the statement alike, are beyond its reach. With a list count of 9 and a stated count of 10, the gap is 1 whether the truth is 9 or 10. Which readout to use is therefore an empirical question per model and task family; the method’s rule (list count unless the list is degenerate) is supported by the measurements of Section 7.2, not by this proposition.

4.2 Behaviour under repetition, changed views and changed models

Joint reporting law.

Fix a complete interface η\eta: model, prompt, schema, setting, cap and view. A call with interface η\eta reports a true object oo with probability qo,ηq_{o,\eta}, and a candidate false object ff (a location where false records tend to appear) with probability qf,ηq_{f,\eta}. Given these propensities, repeated calls with the same η\eta are independent. This joint law, with qq free to depend on every part of η\eta, is the behavioural model; the consequences below use only it, together with conditional independence given the propensities for calls with different interfaces wherever that is stated, and not the explanatory logit parametrization (object, model and view terms) of Appendix A.1. A reported record contributes to the loss only through the matching: emitting a record near oo, producing a match, and adding a match that no other record already provides are different events.

Three consequences are used in the paper. Persistence: for fixed η\eta, the probability of missing oo in all KK calls is (1−qo,η)K(1-q_{o,\eta})^{K}, and averaged over objects it is 𝔼⁡[(1−qo,η)K]\mathbb{E}[(1-q_{o,\eta})^{K}], which tends to the share of objects with q=0q=0. The decay is slow when qq is small for some objects, so at a fixed budget many misses repeat. Diminishing coverage: for calls that are exchangeable given the image, the expected number of targets matched by the union of KK calls is concave in KK; this follows from the submodularity of coverage (Nemhauser et al., 1978) and of matching rank (Lemma 1). The statement concerns raw coverage, not the loss of a constructed set: repeated calls can still remove false records that do not repeat. For example, with 20 true records that are always reported and 80 candidate false records reported independently with probability 0.2, one call has expected E=16E=16 and three-call unanimity has expected E=0.64E=0.64. Confirmation rates: if the records of two calls refer to the same candidate objects and the two calls are conditionally independent given the propensities, a partner call BB confirms a record of call AA with probability

h±=𝔼⁡[qA​qB∣true / false]𝔼⁡[qA∣true / false],h_{\pm}=\frac{\mathbb{E}[q_{A}q_{B}\mid\text{true / false}]}{\mathbb{E}[q_{A}\mid\text{true / false}]},

with h+h_{+} for true records and h−h_{-} for false ones. For a second call with the same interface qB=qAq_{B}=q_{A}, so h=𝔼⁡[qA2]/𝔼⁡[qA]h=\mathbb{E}[q_{A}^{2}]/\mathbb{E}[q_{A}]. A review call that receives the first answer has a different interface and is not covered by this formula.

Proposition 5 (When a different partner is better).

Assume deletion-only confirmation, no match takeover (so Δ​r\Delta r equals the number of true records deleted), no ignore region or all of AA’s false records outside it, and expected counts n+n_{+} (true) and n−n_{-} (false) among AA’s records, with h±Bh^{B}_{\pm} averaged over these records. Then the expected reduction in set error EE (equal costs) from replacing AA by A∩BA\cap B is

G⁡(B)=n−​(1−h−B)−n+​(1−h+B),G(B)=n_{-}\,(1-h_{-}^{B})-n_{+}\,(1-h_{+}^{B}),

and a partner BB beats a same-interface partner A′A^{\prime} iff n−​(h−A′−h−B)>n+​(h+A′−h+B)n_{-}\,(h_{-}^{A^{\prime}}-h_{-}^{B})>n_{+}\,(h_{+}^{A^{\prime}}-h_{+}^{B}).

The partner must reject more of AA’s false records than it loses of AA’s true ones, weighted by their counts. Neither similar overall quality nor a larger separation h+−h−h_{+}-h_{-} is necessary or sufficient: with n+=100n_{+}=100 and n−=10n_{-}=10, the pair (h+,h−)=(0.95,0.85)(h_{+},h_{-})=(0.95,0.85) gives G=−3.5G=-3.5, while the more separated pair (0.5,0)(0.5,0) gives G=−40G=-40; and a weaker partner whose errors avoid AA’s false records can satisfy the inequality. Without the assumptions, the exact relation of Proposition 1 replaces these expectations.

Reports from several views.

Nothing in the chain assumes that a report comes from one call on the whole image. A view is part of the interface η\eta, so a view planner (tiling, the safe decomposition of the companion paper, zoom) produces calls like any other, and their records, mapped to image coordinates, enter the same constructions and losses. Merging the reports of several views is itself a construction: the union of their records, with duplicates in the overlaps removed by the association rule. Confirmation across views is covered by Proposition 2 and Proposition 5 with one change. A view can report only objects that it contains, so for a record lying wholly inside no partner view, h+B=h−B=0h_{+}^{B}=h_{-}^{B}=0: deleting it is a decision about that record’s own p1p_{1}, on which the partner carries no information. A view should therefore confirm or reject only the records it contains. A different view changes the propensities, but it need not share fewer persistent misses: the coverage it adds splits into a gain in how often objects are reported and a gain in complementarity, as for the rescue rate after Proposition 9 (worked example in Appendix A.1). Whether a view helps as a partner is again the inequality of Proposition 5, which also counts its false records.

Proposition 6 (Alarm from disagreement).

Consider a point task in which a record matches a target of the same class within distance θ\theta, with no ignore region, and let EE be its set error. Let U2​θ​(A,B)=|A|+|B|−2​m2​θ​(A,B)U_{2\theta}(A,B)=|A|+|B|-2\,m_{2\theta}(A,B), where m2​θm_{2\theta} is the matching size between two reports when records of the same class are paired within 2​θ2\theta. Then

E⁡(A)+E⁡(B)≥U2​θ​(A,B),E(A)+E(B)\ \geq\ U_{2\theta}(A,B),

hence max⁡{E⁡(A),E⁡(B)}≥12​U2​θ​(A,B)\max\{E(A),E(B)\}\geq\tfrac{1}{2}\,U_{2\theta}(A,B).

The bound needs no labels: when U>0U>0, at least one of the two reports is wrong, although the bound does not say which. Constructed instances attain it, and it can be loose: two identical wrong reports give U=0U=0. The click alarm in our experiments (distance above a share of the longer image side) is an empirical alarm for the hit-in-box loss, evaluated by risk-coverage curves.

4.3 Construction and selection

Fix a feasible family 𝒮A\mathcal{S}_{A} and a loss. Define the oracle risk Ror=𝔼⁡[minS∈𝒮A⁡ℓ⁡(S,Y)]R_{\mathrm{or}}=\mathbb{E}[\min_{S\in\mathcal{S}_{A}}\ell(S,Y)], which uses the truth to pick the best set; the best risk RΦ∗=infg𝔼⁡[ℓ⁡(g⁡(Φ),Y)]R^{*}_{\Phi}=\inf_{g}\mathbb{E}[\ell(g(\Phi),Y)] of a rule that maps features Φ\Phi computed from outputs alone into 𝒮A\mathcal{S}_{A}; and the risk Rg^R_{\hat{g}} of a fitted rule.

Proposition 7 (Risk ordering).

Ror≤RΦ∗≤Rg^R_{\mathrm{or}}\leq R^{*}_{\Phi}\leq R_{\hat{g}}, and

Rg^−Ror=\displaystyle R_{\hat{g}}-R_{\mathrm{or}}=\ (RΦ∗−Ror)⏟information not in ​Φ\displaystyle\underbrace{(R^{*}_{\Phi}-R_{\mathrm{or}})}_{\text{information not in }\Phi}
+(Rg^−RΦ∗)⏟selector and estimation.\displaystyle+\underbrace{(R_{\hat{g}}-R^{*}_{\Phi})}_{\text{selector and estimation}}.

An observed gap between a selector and the oracle bounds the sum but does not apportion it. A rule whose fitting uses labels is a label-fitted output-feature selector: it reads no labels at inference, but its fitting does. The gap concerns a fixed library of calls; it says nothing about what additional calls or a different library would add.

For the family with at most one representative per cluster, which the selectors of Section 7.8 use, the oracle is a maximum matching between clusters and targets and is computed exactly (Proposition 12 in Appendix A); unrestricted matching over all records can exceed it but is not attainable within the family (Section 7.8 reports both).

4.4 Choosing one answer among several calls

A click has one answer, so the constructions above reduce to choosing one point. Let several calls (models, settings, views) give an item a menu AA of candidate points. Group the candidates into clusters, the connected components of the graph that joins two candidates within distance δ\delta; fix one representative per cluster before any choice is made; and let a rule output one representative. For clicks these clusters replace the association rule of Section 3.4. The loss is the miss, 𝟙[y^∉target]\mathbb{1}[\hat{y}\notin\text{target}]. In the GUI-grounding tier of Section 5.1 a scoring model, the scorer, gives each candidate a hit score and compares representatives; Section 7.7 reports it on 600 click items.

Proposition 8 (Three sources of a miss).

For every rule that outputs a representative, the miss rate is exactly F+L+WF+L+W, where FF is the probability that no candidate in AA hits, LL that some candidate hits but no representative does, and WW that some representative hits but the rule outputs one that misses.

The terms locate where a miss arises; they are not independent effects of interventions. With the candidate menu fixed, changing the representatives leaves FF unchanged but can move a miss between LL and WW. With candidates and representatives fixed, changing only the final choice acts on WW. Only changing or enlarging the candidate menu can lower FF, and doing so can change all three terms at once, because a new candidate can also change the clusters, the representatives and the comparison. Section 7.7 measures the three terms separately when a source is added. How much an added candidate lowers FF needs no independence assumption:

Proposition 9 (Coverage of an added source).

Let FF be the probability that every candidate of a menu misses, and ϕ=Pr⁡(an added candidate hits∣every earlier candidate misses)\phi=\Pr(\text{an added candidate hits}\mid\text{every earlier candidate misses}). With the added candidate, the probability becomes F⁡(1−ϕ)F(1-\phi). If the candidates are conditionally independent given per-item hit probabilities q1,…,qkq_{1},\dots,q_{k}, then F=𝔼⁡[∏j=1k(1−qj)]F=\mathbb{E}[\prod_{j=1}^{k}(1-q_{j})].

The relevant quantity is the rescue rate ϕ\phi on the items the existing menu misses, not the added source’s own accuracy or its correlation alone. For the indicators II that some earlier candidate hits and JJ that the added candidate hits, with Pr⁡(I=0)>0\Pr(I=0)>0,

ϕ=Pr⁡(J=1∣I=0)=𝔼⁡[J]−Cov⁡(I,J)1−𝔼⁡[I],\phi=\Pr(J=1\mid I=0)=\mathbb{E}[J]-\frac{\mathrm{Cov}(I,J)}{1-\mathbb{E}[I]},

the binary form of the decomposition into reporting rate and complementarity for views (Appendix A.1). At equal hit rates, lower covariance raises the rescue rate; when hit rates differ, both terms matter. Persistence makes the covariance of a repeated call with the same interface large, which is why a repeat tends to rescue little, but a weak partner can rescue less than a repeat. Section 7.7 therefore measures ϕ\phi for each tested source.

Proposition 10 (Net effect of a switch).

Let a base rule output bb, and let an action replace bb by gg on a set TT of items decided from outputs. With eT=Pr⁡(b​ misses∣T)e_{T}=\Pr(b\text{ misses}\mid T), the repair rate rfix=Pr⁡(g​ hits∣b​ misses,T)r_{\mathrm{fix}}=\Pr(g\text{ hits}\mid b\text{ misses},T) and the break rate rbrk=Pr⁡(g​ misses∣b​ hits,T)r_{\mathrm{brk}}=\Pr(g\text{ misses}\mid b\text{ hits},T), the miss rate falls by exactly

Pr⁡(T)​[eT​rfix−(1−eT)​rbrk].\Pr(T)\,\big[\,e_{T}\,r_{\mathrm{fix}}-(1-e_{T})\,r_{\mathrm{brk}}\,\big].

If, within an event U⊇TU\supseteq T, membership in TT is independent of whether bb misses, then eT=Pr⁡(b​ misses∣U)e_{T}=\Pr(b\text{ misses}\mid U).

This is the click counterpart of Proposition 2: an action pays when the errors it repairs outweigh the correct answers it breaks, counted on the items it touches. Disagreement alone does not say which candidate is wrong (Proposition 6 bounds the sum of two errors, not the base error), so where to act is an empirical question. Where the base miss rate eTe_{T} is low, as on items whose candidates agree, an action must break very few correct answers to pay: with eT=5.8%e_{T}=5.8\%, fewer than about 3.1% if it repairs half of the misses (Section 7.7 measures eTe_{T} with and without an alarm). The scorer is a design choice of the configuration and not a consequence of the theory: choosing the best of NsN_{\mathrm{s}} candidate scorers to within a miss-rate gap εs\varepsilon_{\mathrm{s}} with probability 1−βs1-\beta_{\mathrm{s}} takes on the order of log⁡(Ns/βs)/εs2\log(N_{\mathrm{s}}/\beta_{\mathrm{s}})/\varepsilon_{\mathrm{s}}^{2} labelled items under independent sampling, so the pipeline ships one scorer and does not choose it per task.

4.5 What outputs alone can and cannot certify

Proposition 11 (No output-only certificate).

Fix a reported set SS, a loss LL and a tolerance ϵ\epsilon. Suppose two admissible worlds induce the same law PP of the observable output history HH, while L⁡(S,Y0)≤ϵL(S,Y_{0})\leq\epsilon in the first and L⁡(S,Y1)>ϵL(S,Y_{1})>\epsilon in the second. Then every output-only acceptance rule a⁡(H)∈[0,1]a(H)\in[0,1], possibly randomized, accepts with the same probability in both worlds, so no such rule can accept with probability at least 1−β1-\beta in the first world and at most α\alpha in the second if α+β<1\alpha+\beta<1. More generally, P1​(accept)≥P0​(accept)−TV⁡(P0,P1)P_{1}(\text{accept})\geq P_{0}(\text{accept})-\mathrm{TV}(P_{0},P_{1}), where TV\mathrm{TV} is the total variation distance.

The same argument applies to any property of YY on which two such worlds disagree, for example whether L⁡(S,Y)<L⁡(S′,Y)L(S,Y)<L(S^{\prime},Y) for two reports SS and S′S^{\prime}, so which of two reports is more accurate cannot be certified from outputs alone either. The argument is the two-point method of minimax lower bounds (Tsybakov, 2009); methods that estimate accuracy from the agreement of several classifiers without labels (Platanios et al., 2014) rely on assumptions, such as weakly dependent errors, that rule such pairs out. Such pairs arise from objects that a model rarely reports. If the bad world adds one target that each of KK calls reports with probability at most ϑ\vartheta, given the earlier output, and the target does not change the rest of the output, then TV⁡(P0,P1)≤K​ϑ\mathrm{TV}(P_{0},P_{1})\leq K\vartheta. Any test’s advantage in telling the two worlds apart, the difference between its acceptance probabilities in them, is then at most K​ϑK\vartheta (with equal priors, the best probability of naming the right world is (1+TV)/2(1+\mathrm{TV})/2), and no test is reliable uniformly over admissible classes in which ϑ\vartheta can be arbitrarily small. The practical reading: agreement alone does not certify correctness. This does not prevent running a default procedure, ordering interfaces under explicit assumptions tested on other data, as the companion paper does for decomposition (Shi et al., 2026), or operating a configuration chosen on source data without new labels.

Corollary 1 (Sign of a count gap).

Suppose that, for a given report SS, some admissible world has |S|>n|S|>n, and that the admissible worlds are closed under adding any number of targets that no interface reports and that do not change the rest of the output. Then the sign of |S|−n|S|-n is not determined by the outputs: that world has the same output law as one in which SS under-counts. (This differs from the sign of a recall gain between two interfaces, which assumptions such as monotonicity in tokens per object can fix.)

Without further information, neither deleting unconfirmed records nor keeping them dominates for a count objective. Our count procedure keeps them, a conservative choice whose quality we evaluate empirically.

5 Method: A Default Pipeline with Stated Inputs

The default pipeline of FSR turns an image, a task specification and a budget into a final set, a task answer, a status and an alarm score; it needs no labels from the target task. A summary table in Section 8 gives when each component helps, its measured effect and its cost. Every input it uses comes from one of three named sources, or is computed from the current responses: [task] the task specification and budget given by the user (classes, alias map, matching rule, loss); [config] the shipped configuration, a fixed file released with the code (config/default_pipeline.json) whose values were chosen on our evaluation data and are carried unchanged to new images; and [labels] optional labelled images. No step requires the user to know p1p_{1}, a partner’s quality or the current F1. Algorithm 1 gives the procedure; its comments name the steps described below. Steps 1 to 6 repair the report, the optional label rule of Step 7 judges between configurations, and the alarm of Step 8 detects errors. Section 5.1 adds the GUI-grounding tier, a second tier for clicks that combines several models, and Section 5.2 describes how the model behind these steps was revised.

Inputs [task, config].

The task fixes the class vocabulary 𝒞τ\mathcal{C}_{\tau}, the alias map ατ\alpha_{\tau} (for example {diamond, rhombus, rotated square} ↦\mapsto square), the matching rule ρτ\rho_{\tau} of Table 2, the ignore region Ωτ\Omega_{\tau} and the loss ℓτ\ell_{\tau}. The loss selects the construction in Step 5. The user also gives a budget per item. The shipped configuration fixes everything else that the algorithm calls a value: the prompt, the reporting interface and reasoning setting per model and loss (Table 4), the four flag thresholds, the recovery request, the view settings, the construction per loss, the alarm partner, the default alarm threshold, and the models, settings, distance, scorer and number of compared clusters of Algorithm 2. For counts, a model known to write degenerate lists at its lowest setting (Gemini 3.8) is run at its default setting (Section 7.3).

Steps 1 and 2: dispatch and decode.

Step 1 is a dispatcher, not one fixed request: what is shared across tasks is the chain of records, losses and readouts, not one output format. For set tasks scored by F1 the shipped configuration may select the regions interface, in which the model returns one row per region of a fixed coordinate registry (Appendix D). The count request asks for one JSON object in which the list of records comes first and counts_by_type follows, declared “for the shapes you listed” (Appendix D gives the prompt). The allowed class names are listed in the format; the model scans row by row from top to bottom and uses its native coordinate frame (0 to 1000 for GPT and Gemini; pixels for Sonnet, with the image pre-resized so that the provider does not resize it again). No grid, ticks or markers are drawn. The decoder keeps every recoverable record in the audit collection ZallZ^{\mathrm{all}} and passes the valid ones, after the alias map, to the delivered collection ZZ (Section 3). It sets four degeneracy flags on the list: more than 10% of records without a valid class; a list length outside [0.5,1.5][0.5,1.5] times the stated total; more than 10% repeated coordinates; and the finish reason “length”.

Step 3: bounded recovery.

The two kinds of failure get different recoveries. A transport failure, in which the call did not return, is a property of the connection and is resent unchanged. A flagged response is a property of how the model wrote this report, and such errors tend to recur, consistent with Section 4.2: in our detection experiments, resending a request whose flag had already repeated cleared the flag in 14.7% of cases, while changing the request cleared it in 58.8%. The change was a follow-up that attached the previous answer and asked for the complete answer under the same contract, or, for reports organised by image region, a new request for the flagged regions only. The pipeline sends the first kind of follow-up, once. If the follow-up still carries a flag, the first response is kept with its flags, and Step 6 decides how to read it. Every attempt enters the cost. The replay at the end of this section reports how often recovery was triggered and what the stored follow-ups changed.

Step 4: views.

For clicks we use a re-grounding strategy in the style of the ReGround method that Li et al. (2025b) evaluate. The first call gives a point on the whole screenshot. A crop one third of the screenshot’s width and height, centred on that point and shifted to stay inside the image, is sent at native pixels, and the second call gives the point in the crop. If the second call gives no point, the first point is kept; if the first call gives no point, there is nothing to zoom on and the answer is no point, which counts as a miss. Using agreement to decide when to zoom costs more and is not more accurate (Section 7.5). For sets and counts, the pipeline does not plan views itself: it works on whatever reports it is given. By default it sends the whole image. When a view planner is configured, for example a tiling scheme or the companion paper’s safe decomposition, which places every target wholly inside some view, with neighbouring views overlapping by one object and no view having fewer tokens per object than the whole image, and cannot lower expected recall under that paper’s monotonicity assumptions (Shi et al., 2026), each view is one call, its records are mapped to image coordinates, and Step 5 merges them. We computed the apparent size of every annotated object in the whole-image calls on SCP-dense, DocLayNet, DOTA and SKU-110K, using the input geometry measured in the companion paper and its released calibration data (32-pixel tokens for GPT-6.1, 28-pixel tokens for Sonnet 5.5, a fixed grid of about 1,090 tokens for Gemini 3.8). The median object spans 0.62 to 1.43 tokens across its shorter side (the companion paper measures size as the square root of the area, which is never smaller). Below that paper’s design value of S⋆=1.5S^{\star}=1.5 fall 55% to 79% of objects on the three detection sources and every shape on SCP-dense; yet GPT-6.1 and Sonnet 5.5 write nearly exact lists on SCP-dense. The companion paper likewise finds that these model families reach half recall at well under one token per object side. A fixed threshold would decompose images whose whole-image report is already complete, so when to call a planner is a property of the model and the task that the configuration supplies. These sizes come from the annotations and inform only this design choice; the pipeline reads no annotation at run time. Section 7.5 reports how the pipeline handles reports from four crops, and how our own tiling arm, which did not meet the safe condition, fared on large objects.

Step 5: construction.

The construction is chosen per loss (Table 4). Records of different calls are associated without labels (Table 2): boxes of the same class with IoU ≥0.5\geq 0.5, screen elements at IoU ≥0.5\geq 0.5 without class, and points of the same class within the task’s tolerance. On over-reporting task families and set error, three calls are made and a record is kept only if all three report it, with its coordinates averaged over the three. Everywhere else a single call is delivered without deletion. Over- or under-reporting is a property of the task family, shipped with the configuration from our evaluation; the user does not supply it. Coordinate averaging is on by default because its contribution is positive in 37 of 54 base/partner pairs and negative in 13 (Section 7.4); the deletion-only variant is in the menu. Reports of several views are first merged into one report: the union of their records, where a record is dropped if it is associated with a record already kept from another view (a duplicate in an overlap). When reports from different views confirm one another, a view can confirm or reject only records that lie wholly inside it; a record that no partner view contains is kept (Section 4.2). A call that still has no readable answer after recovery counts as an empty report, so three-call unanimity keeps nothing on that image; this is the construction we evaluated, and dropping such a call from the support count is in the menu.

Step 6: readout.

The answer is read from the final set. For counts it is the list count of SS, the number of records of each class. When the list behind SS carries a degeneracy flag and the response stated counts, the answer falls back to the stated count dd, and the status says so (count_from_statement); a flagged list without stated counts keeps the list count and its flag. With several views, each response states counts for its own crop, and overlapping views would count shared objects twice; stated counts are therefore never combined across views, and a flagged merged list keeps the list count, with the status saying that no stated count was used. The fallback changes only the count: SS itself is not repaired, so the count and the set each carry their own status. The flags, not the readout gap, trigger the fallback, because a gap shows that the two readouts disagree without saying which is right (Proposition 4).

A second model [config], optional.

When a second model is configured, its default role is the alarm of Step 8: its answer is compared with the user’s, and items where they disagree by more than a threshold are flagged. The disagreement disτ\mathrm{dis}_{\tau} is the summed per-class difference of the two answers for counts, the number of records not associated across the two answers for sets (Table 2), and the distance between the two points as a share of the longer image side for clicks, where a missing point always raises the alarm. The partner is fixed by a rule (GPT-6.1 and Sonnet 5.5: Gemini 3.8; Gemini 3.8: Sonnet 5.5), which picks the cheapest other model per click call (Appendix D), and the threshold δ\delta is a point the user picks on the risk-coverage curve (Section 7.6; shipped default 1.5%). Using the second model to confirm records is a menu option, chosen with labels or a shipped family-level ranking rather than as a zero-label default, because it is worse only in cells where the user’s own model is the strongest (Section 7.9).

Step 7: optional labels [labels].

Labels are never required. With fewer than three labelled images the pipeline keeps the shipped default and reports the labelled error. With three or more, it switches to another configuration from the menu only if that configuration’s mean advantage over the labelled images, paired by image, minus one standard error is positive. Section 7.4 evaluates this rule for the decision to delete unconfirmed records. With 5 to 10 labelled images it may also fit the record gate, a logistic selector on output features (Section 7.8). Certifying the accuracy of a pipeline on a population is a separate service that needs its own labelled sample.

Step 8: delivery.

The pipeline returns the final set SS, the answer y^\hat{y}, the readout branch, the status σ\sigma (L1 to L3, flags, recovery used, views used), the alarm score when a second report exists, and the cost of every attempt.

One entry point, replayed on stored calls.

The repository implements Steps 1 to 6 and 8 of Algorithm 1 for counts, sets and single-model clicks, including merging views and cross-view confirmation, as a single entry point (fsr_pipeline/) whose branches read only the task specification, the shipped configuration and the responses a client returns; the label rule of Step 7 is a function in the same module, and the record gate is fitted by the analysis code of Section 7.8. Algorithm 2 runs as a separate function (gui/code/decision.py), and the per-model F1 configuration is a key of the shipped configuration file evaluated by the analysis of Section 7.9; neither is a branch of this entry point. A replay client serves the stored responses of this paper instead of calling a model. A request for which nothing was stored, such as a follow-up that was never sent, returns “unavailable”, and the pipeline continues on its documented branch. Run on raw responses, the entry point reproduces the component analyses: the count errors of Sections 7.2 and 7.3, the click hit rates after two-stage zoom of Section 7.5, and, with recovery switched off, the set error of the shipped construction in all 18 transfer cells to within 0.07 per image, a difference that comes from the 0.1-pixel coordinate rounding of the component analysis. Follow-ups were stored for a sample of flagged detection calls. In the 18 set cells, 171 image runs had at least one flagged call; a stored follow-up cleared the flag in 24 of them, and replaying these changes set error by at most 0.55 per image in any cell. No follow-ups were stored for the count experiments, where 51 runs were flagged, so their results are those of the first call. Synthetic boundary cases go through the same code, and each produces an answer, a readout branch and a status: an empty or unreadable response, truncated JSON, a list without stated counts, a degenerate list with and without stated counts, two transport failures in a row, one unreadable call among three, and a click with no first point or no point in the crop. The replay output is released with the analysis outputs (pipeline_replay.json).

5.1 GUI grounding: clicks from several models

Algorithm 1 delivers one model’s two-stage zoom point. When the per-item budget covers the planned worst case of a second tier, the pipeline offers one built on the three sources of a miss (Proposition 8); its mean cost is about 3.2 times that of one zoom. Its run-time inputs are the image, the instruction and the budget; it reads no target label and does not abstain. The models, their settings, the distance δ\delta, the scorer and the number of compared clusters come from the shipped configuration [config].

Algorithm 2 gives the steps, organised by Proposition 8. Generation enlarges the candidate menu, which is the only way to lower FF; Section 7.7 measures the rescue rate of each source on the others’ misses (Proposition 9). The representative step fixes which member of each cluster can be output, and the comparison chooses among representatives, so these two steps divide the remaining misses between LL and WW. The comparison runs only on items with an alarm, where the measured miss rate of the scorer’s choice is highest (Sections 4.4 and 7.7); items whose candidates form one cluster keep that cluster’s representative. The scorer’s hit score is used only to rank. The registry makes the point that is scored, drawn, compared and returned the same point: every step refers to a candidate by its identifier, and the code asserts that the coordinates drawn for the scorer equal those returned. If a call fails, the procedure continues with the remaining candidates. It returns no point only when no candidate is available; a missing point counts as a miss, and every returned point is scored by the hit-in-target rule. The budget selects among planned call schedules before inference: the tier runs only if the budget covers its planned worst case of 15 calls at per-call output caps of 16,384 tokens at the lowest setting and 32,768 at the default. Technical retries are outside this bound, and the per-item costs we report are realized averages over all attempts, retries included. The rules are implemented as one deterministic function over stored or live responses (gui/code/decision.py in the release), with request builders for each step; with the evaluation script, run on the stored responses, it regenerates the results of Section 7.7.

5.2 Revising the model from failed predictions

The theory was built by iteration, and the iteration is part of the method. A model is stated, a consequence is derived and tested, and when a prediction fails we record three things: which assumption failed and how we know; how the revised assumption was checked directly; and what new consequence the revision predicts, and whether it holds. Table 5 lists the five revisions that shaped the final theory. Each row names the kind of evidence: an exact identity, a controlled comparison of interventions on the same images, or an association observed across cells or records.

6 Experimental Setup

Models and settings.

The main experiments use three API models: GPT-6.1 (OpenAI), Claude Sonnet 5.5 (Anthropic) and Gemini 3.8 Flash (Google), written Sonnet 5.5 and Gemini 3.8. Pilots and the controlled-scene experiments also use GPT-5.6 and Opus 5.5, and an open-weight model, Qwen3-VL-235B, is tested in the pilots and on the readout tasks. Each call uses either the lowest reasoning setting the API offers or the default setting. Setting labels do not match behaviour, and we report what was measured (Appendix C). Three facts matter for interpretation. First, the default setting also doubled the output cap (16,384 to 32,768 tokens); three runs separate the two: the Gemini 3.8 runs of Section 7.3, a 90-call 16k control on the detection sources, and a 16k control on controlled scenes. Second, Sonnet 5.5’s reasoning share at its default setting varies by task: 0% to 23% of calls in the reasoning experiment (dense scenes, FSC-147, screens) and 0% to 90% across detection cells; we attribute a Sonnet result to reasoning only where most of its calls reasoned. Reasoning tokens are read from the usage fields of every call after the pilots (Qwen3-VL is an instruct model and reports none); the two pilots logged no thinking tokens for the Claude models. Third, Gemini 3.8 at its lowest setting still reasoned on click and point outputs (about 99% of GUI click calls), so its click results at the lowest setting include reasoning. GPT-6.1’s lowest setting is reasoning_effort=low, and most of its calls carry some reasoning tokens. Images sent to Sonnet 5.5 were resized to at most 1,568 pixels on the long side and 1.15 megapixels (by our code, or in the detection experiment by the provider), and images sent to the other models to at most 2,048 pixels; for Sonnet 5.5 this is below the 2,576-pixel long edge measured for it in the companion paper (Shi et al., 2026).

Data.

The synthetic counting probe (SCP) has 100 images of 1024×10241024\times 1024 pixels with five shape classes and 15 to 80 shapes each (mean 47.6), drawn over clutter lines; SCP-dense uses the same generator with 50 images of 121 to 200 smaller shapes (mean 164.3). Labels are exact. Photographs, aerial images and document pages come from PixMo-Count (100 images, 2 to 10 objects), FSC-147 (100 images in three size strata for the readout and tiling experiments, and 60 further images for the detection experiment), and 60 images each from SKU-110K, DOTA v1.0 and DocLayNet v1.2 (three classes). Screen data are 200 ScreenSpot-Pro and 60 ScreenSpot-v2 click items, 60 GroundCUA screens and 60 ScreenParse screens; the click experiment of Section 7.7 adds 600 further ScreenSpot-Pro click items, sampled with a fixed seed and sharing no item and no screenshot with the 260 click items. The controlled-scene experiments add 96 procedurally drawn scenes with 16 to 384 targets each. A readout experiment on aerial and document images adds 30 DOTA v1.0 windows and 50 DocLayNet pages (financial reports, tenders and laws), selected with the annotations to contain at least three (DOTA) or four (DocLayNet) classes and at least 30 or 20 objects, disjoint from the detection images. In total the experiments use 1,746 images with 54,475 annotated targets (each click item counts as one target). We refer to SKU-110K, DOTA, DocLayNet and FSC-147 as the detection sources and to GroundCUA and ScreenParse as the screen sources.

Experiments.

Table 6 lists the experiments that the results draw on. Every call of these experiments, including smoke tests, pilots and retries, is stored with its raw response; the full registry with costs is in Appendix C. Merges of existing calls (intersections, unanimity, cross-model constructions) are deterministic post-processing of stored responses: the same items are re-scored under a changed construction.

Statistics.

Intervals are 95% paired bootstrap intervals over images (4,000 resamples unless stated), with relative changes computed on means. “Significant” means the interval excludes 0. Comparisons of two click flows on the same items also report the items repaired and broken and an exact McNemar test, with Holm adjustment where two comparisons share a claim. Fold assignments and random draws use seeds derived from SHA-256 of a fixed string and are persisted, so every table regenerates byte-identically from the saved responses with one script. Costs count every attempted call at list prices, with one exception: when the 600-item click run was interrupted and resumed, at most 8 requests were in flight without a stored response, at most about $0.05, which is not in the totals.

7 Results

The results follow the three problems of Section 1: a comparison with common practice (Section 7.1), repairing reports (Sections 7.2 to 7.5), detecting errors (Section 7.6), repairing a click by choosing among several models (Section 7.7), and judging which report or configuration is more accurate (Sections 7.8 and 7.9). Each table caption states the operation, the comparator, the loss and any label use.

7.1 Against common practice

The comparisons in this subsection use the stored calls of the earlier experiments; the 600-item click evaluation is in Section 7.7.

Table 7 compares the defaults of Section 5 with the remedies practitioners use most, on the same stored calls. The pattern follows the three problems. Self-consistency repeats the same source of evidence, so its gains are small: the median of three stated counts helps GPT-6.1 by 23% and the other two models by about 1%, at three times the cost, and a vote of three clicks changes the miss rate by −4.5%-4.5\% to +2.5%+2.5\%. Uncertainty-gated zoom, which zooms only when two clicks of the same model disagree, inherits the same weakness, because persistent errors rarely produce disagreement; it gains 13% for Gemini 3.8 and nothing significant for the other two. The remedies that change the information win: reading the list cuts dense-count error by 85% and 99% for about the cost of one call, and zooming every item cuts the miss rate by 45% and 65% for less than a three-click vote. For set error, three-call unanimity with averaged coordinates improves 9 of the 15 over-reporting cells (median −9.6%-9.6\%), against −2.9%-2.9\% for majority vote and −3.7%-3.7\% for box fusion, and it beats box fusion directly in 11 of the 15 cells and is not significantly worse in any. For detecting missed clicks at the same distance threshold, a second model catches 1.9 to 3.5 times the share of errors that a second call of the same model catches, while flagging more items (Section 7.6).

7.2 Repair the readout: read the list, not the number

Same response, two answers.

Figure 3 shows one response in full. When a list-first response has both a list and stated counts, the list length misses the true total by 0.04 objects on average for GPT-6.1 and 0.02 for Sonnet 5.5, while the stated totals miss by 7.78 and 10.48 (Table 8, last row). Reading per-type counts from the list (the list count) instead of the stated counts in the same response cuts per-type count error by 75.6% (GPT-6.1) and 77.7% (Sonnet 5.5) under a count-first prompt, and by 84.2% and 70.7% under the list-first prompt. Generation is held fixed in these comparisons, so the gain is a readout effect: the model’s list carries information that its own summary loses.

The gap grows with the length of a multi-type list.

Figure 4 (values in Table B.1) repeats the same-response comparison on four datasets. On PixMo (6 objects per image, one class) and FSC-147 (43.8 objects, one class), the stated total tracks the list for GPT-6.1 and Sonnet 5.5 and the difference is not significant. On SCP (47.6 objects, five classes) the list count is better by 44% for GPT-6.1 and by 98.5% for Sonnet 5.5, whose stated per-type counts are 65 times as far from the truth as its list. On SCP-dense (164.3 objects) both models gain 76% to 78%. The gap therefore appears when the stated count must summarize a long list across several classes.

Aliases and protocol.

In list-first responses, Sonnet 5.5 wrote 258 “diamond” records across 50 images although the format listed the allowed names. The declared alias map, applied to the same list, takes its error from 5.42 to 0.42 (−92.3%-92.3\%). The prompt alone does not do this: the map is part of the task, and the decoder applies it. Holding the mapped readout fixed, list-first lists are better than count-first lists by 39.4% for GPT-6.1 and 92.3% for Sonnet 5.5. The complete protocol, compared with the stated count of a count-first response, cuts error by 85.2% [−89.1,−80.3][-89.1,-80.3] for GPT-6.1 and 98.8% [−99.5,−98.1][-99.5,-98.1] for Sonnet 5.5. For Gemini 3.8 at its lowest setting the change is +15.6%+15.6\% [−5.3,39.4][-5.3,39.4], not significant: the degeneracy check routes 40 of its 50 responses to the stated count. These are effects of the reporting and decoding protocol. The same-response and same-list comparisons isolate the readout and the alias map; the full protocol also changes how the list is generated.

Aerial and document images with several classes.

The readout repair needs a gap to work with. We ran both prompts on 30 DOTA windows and 50 DocLayNet pages chosen to contain several classes and many objects (Table 9; 574 calls). There the lists themselves miss objects: GPT-6.1 and Sonnet 5.5 list 68% to 88% of the true objects. The stated count also stays close to the list count of the same response, differing by 0.1 to 7.4 per image against per-type errors of 5 to 46. Switching readouts can change the error by at most this gap (Proposition 4), so the change in the same response is small: none for GPT-6.1, and −13.5%-13.5\% and −19.9%-19.9\% for Sonnet 5.5. The full list-first protocol, here without the recovery step, changes count error by +0.4%+0.4\% and −2.4%-2.4\% for GPT-6.1 and by −15.7%-15.7\% and −20.1%-20.1\% for Sonnet 5.5, intervals reaching zero. Gemini 3.8 at its lowest setting again writes degenerate lists; the fallback to the stated count holds its change to +18.0%+18.0\% and −7.9%-7.9\%, both not significant, and at its default setting, the shipped configuration, it changes count error, together with the setting, by −28.2%-28.2\% on DOTA (interval reaching zero) and by −25.8%-25.8\% on DocLayNet. The two kinds of scene differ in where the error sits. On dense synthetic scenes the lists are nearly complete and the statement loses information, so the readout repairs most of the error; on these aerial and document images most of the error is already in the list, so switching between the two readouts cannot remove it. The label-free readout gap tells the two cases apart in one direction: when it is small, switching readouts cannot matter (Proposition 4).

7.3 Repair the readout when the list degenerates

Gemini 3.8 at its lowest setting writes long lists in which most records lack a valid class and some coordinates repeat, so the list count is far worse than its stated count (+182.5%+182.5\% in the same response; Figure 4). The four-part degeneracy check of Section 5 flags 45 of its 50 dense-scene lists. For 40 of them the readout falls back to the stated count; the other 5 have no stated count and keep the list count with a status flag. On the GPT-6.1 and Sonnet 5.5 list-first responses it flags none.

For Gemini 3.8, degeneration depends mainly on the reasoning setting. At the same 16k output cap, Gemini 3.8’s default setting reduces flagged lists from 90% to 12% and the readout error from 52.80 to 24.52 (−53.6%-53.6\% [−72.4,−29.5][-72.4,-29.5]; Table 10). Doubling the cap to 32k gives a point estimate of 15.44, a further change that is not significant. Even then, Gemini 3.8’s dense-count error is about ten times GPT-6.1’s, and none of its 50 counts is exact. Strict JSON parsing fails for 70% to 78% of Gemini 3.8 responses at every setting, so the declared record salvage of Section 3.5 is a necessary part of the decoder, and its share is reported.

On the list-first responses of the readout experiment, applying the same check to existing responses recovers 68% (SCP) and 58% (SCP-dense) of Gemini 3.8’s error relative to reading its list, and 42% relative to the stated count on FSC-147. For Sonnet 5.5, whose lists are not degenerate, the cost of the check reaches +23%+23\% on SCP and +13%+13\% on SCP-dense (not significant; intervals [0,57][0,57] and [0,26][0,26]). On the open model Qwen3-VL, with thresholds unchanged, it lowers SCP-dense error by 7% [−13,−1][-13,-1] relative to the stated count. Gemini 3.8’s missing class fields follow a pattern: a record is more likely to omit its type when the previous record has the same type, and a row-by-row scan that interleaves types cuts its count error by 60%, while grouping by type makes it worse.

7.4 Repair the set: delete below the threshold, keep geometry separate

Deletion and geometry, measured separately.

Table 11 (per-pair values in Table B.2) splits the effect of confirming a base call with a partner call into the selection term of Proposition 1 and the geometry term of Proposition 3, for 54 base/partner pairs on six sources. Both identities hold exactly on every image, so the selection term of a pair has the sign of 1−2​p11-2p_{1} by construction (Figure 5a). What the data add is where p1p_{1} lies: 0.00 to 0.39 on SKU-110K and 0.05 to 0.22 on DOTA, where deletion removes 4 to 68 errors per image, against 0.39 to 0.90 on FSC-147. On FSC-147, where models under-report, p1p_{1} is 0.39 to 0.90 and deletion hurts in 7 of 9 pairs, which is why counting families keep a single call. Coordinate averaging is positive in 37 pairs and negative in 13. In two pairs it reverses the sign of the deletion-only result: DocLayNet with GPT-6.1 confirmed by Sonnet 5.5 (selection +0.80+0.80, geometry −1.10-1.10 per image) and GroundCUA with Sonnet 5.5 confirmed by itself (selection −0.87-0.87, geometry +1.20+1.20). These are the two pairs in which an earlier check of the threshold on intersections with averaged coordinates failed; separating the terms accounts for both.

The threshold from a few labels.

The useful question is whether p1p_{1} measured on a handful of labelled images predicts what deletion will do on other images. For each pair we drew 5 labelled images 200 times, estimated p1p_{1} on them, and predicted from Proposition 2 whether deleting unconfirmed records lowers set error on the other 55 images of the pair. The prediction is right in 83% of draws (80% with 3 labelled images, 87% with 10), and the loss against the better decision on the other images is 0.33 errors per image (0.48 and 0.15). The shipped family default alone, which deletes on over-reporting families and keeps on FSC-147 without any label, is right in 85% of draws with a loss of 0.43. The label rule of Step 7 combines the two: it starts from the family default and switches only if the labelled images favour the other decision by more than one standard error. It is right in 86%, 87% and 88% of draws with 3, 5 and 10 labelled images, with losses of 0.22, 0.17 and 0.10 errors per image. In the 8 pairs whose p1p_{1} lies within 0.1 of 1/21/2, the gain from deleting is small and its sign is noisy: the plain threshold is right in 47% of draws there, and the family default and the Step 7 rule, which lean towards deletion, in 34% and 37%. Table 11 gives the share by source.

Which partner helps.

Proposition 5 says a partner helps if it rejects more of the base call’s false records than it loses of the true ones.
