Cross-model partners separate the two better than same-model partners in 32 of 36 base/partner comparisons on the detection and screen-parsing sources. The four exceptions are GPT-6.1’s two much weaker partners on FSC-147, and Gemini 3.8 confirming Sonnet 5.5 on FSC-147 and SKU-110K, where Gemini 3.8 confirms few of Sonnet 5.5’s true records. The misses are consistent with a component shared across models: of the objects that GPT-6.1, the highest-recall model, misses in all three of its calls, a single call of either other model recovers only 0.7% to 9% on SKU-110K, DOTA and FSC-147, and 18% to 26% on DocLayNet. New information flows mainly from higher-recall to lower-recall models.

7.5 Repair the view; fixes that do not help

Zoom and tiles.

On ScreenSpot-Pro (200 items), two-stage zoom (Step 4) raises the click hit rate from 64.5% to 87.5% for Gemini 3.8 (+23+23 points [16.5,29.5][16.5,29.5], a 65% cut in the miss rate) and from 78% to 87% for Sonnet 5.5 (+9+9 [5,13.5][5,13.5], a 41% cut; 45% on the 196 items that every arm of Table 7 answered); for GPT-6.1, 88.5% to 90.0% is not significant. Zooming only when two different models disagree, a cross-model version of the gated zoom in Table 7, is less accurate than zooming every item for Sonnet 5.5 (2.3 to 2.7 points) and Gemini 3.8 (9.6 to 12.3 points), not significantly different for GPT-6.1, and more expensive. Our tiling arm on FSC-147 used 2×22\times 2 crops that overlap by 10% of the side, each enlarged 2×2\times and sent in a separate call. It raises the tokens per object side for every object, but its overlap is smaller than one object for the larger objects (median exemplar side 17.5% of the image side in the largest third), so it does not meet the companion paper’s safe-decomposition condition that every target lie inside some view (Shi et al., 2026). The results follow that condition. On the smallest third of images, Sonnet 5.5’s count error falls by 70% against whole-image lists; on the largest third, where many objects lie wholly inside no crop, GPT-6.1’s rises by 78%; over all images Sonnet 5.5’s change (−21%-21\%, [−50,27][-50,27]) is not significant. The small-object gain mixes more tokens per object with less content per call, and the large-object loss is consistent with objects that no crop contains rather than with object size as such. On screens, where tiles overlap by 6%, objects cut by a tile boundary lose 0.16 to 0.42 in report probability in all 6 cells, and separate calls per tile beat one call with several tiles for GPT-6.1 (−15%-15\%, [−23,−5][-23,-5]). For native-resolution click crops, downscaling lowers Sonnet 5.5’s hit rate by 9 points [3,16][3,16], the loss for GPT-6.1 reaches 3 points ([0,7][0,7], not significant), Gemini 3.8 shows no significant response to resizing, consistent with the fixed token grid measured for it in the companion paper, and enlarging these crops does not help.

Reports from a view planner.

In the crop calls of the Review experiment (Table 6) the pipeline receives, for each image, a whole-image report and four reports from four native-resolution crops (6% overlap, one call per crop), on 30 GroundCUA screens and 30 SKU-110K images, scored at IoU ≥0.5\geq 0.5 without class. Merging the four crop reports alone lowers set error relative to one whole-image call for GPT-6.1 on screens (−19.4%-19.4\% [−27.5,−10.6][-27.5,-10.6]) and for Sonnet 5.5 on SKU-110K (−64.0%-64.0\% [−70.6,−56.6][-70.6,-56.6]), raises it for Sonnet 5.5 on screens (+44.9%+44.9\%) and for Gemini 3.8 on SKU-110K (+24.7%+24.7\%), and is not significant in the other two cells. Confirming the whole-image report with the merged crops under the shipped rule, in which a crop confirms or rejects only the records it contains wholly, lowers set error in 4 of 6 cells: GPT-6.1 (−22.8%-22.8\%) and Gemini 3.8 (−20.3%-20.3\%) on screens, and GPT-6.1 (−45.5%-45.5\%) and Sonnet 5.5 (−36.6%-36.6\%) on SKU-110K. In these 4 cells it is also better than confirmation by a second whole-image call (−11.8%-11.8\% to −22.6%-22.6\%), and better than the shipped three-call unanimity in 3 of them (−8.0%-8.0\% to −20.2%-20.2\%; Gemini 3.8 on screens −4.7%-4.7\%, not significant), at the price of five calls instead of three. In the other two cells it raises set error: Sonnet 5.5 on screens (+12.9%+12.9\%) and Gemini 3.8 on SKU-110K (+37.9%+37.9\%). The threshold of Proposition 2 accounts for both groups. Among the whole-image records that the crops do not confirm, the share matched to a true object (p1p_{1}) is 0.03 to 0.24 in the four cells where confirmation helps, and 0.62 and 0.76 in the two where it hurts, as the identity requires. The plain rule, in which every record needs confirmation, differs from the shipped rule by at most 4 percentage points, because with a 6% overlap few records lie wholly inside no crop.

Grids and coordinates.

On SCP, the systematic coordinate offset of current models is at most 0.3 pixels, with slope 1.000 and spread 0.9 to 1.5 pixels, against a matching tolerance of 30 pixels. A grid, ticks or cell labels therefore have no coordinate error to correct: in every arm, localization changes by at most 0.23 pixels, and at the lowest setting they do not significantly change detection for GPT-6.1 and Sonnet 5.5. For Gemini 3.8 at its lowest setting, a grid lowers set error by 3.5 per image by reducing records that omit their class, and a row-by-row scan lowers it by 11.5; at its default setting the grid makes detection and localization slightly worse. “No overlay” is therefore the shipped default, chosen from these measurements; the theory does not forbid an overlay from helping a model whose list format it changes. Markers also make Sonnet 5.5 write “diamond” more often (+0.3+0.3 per image). An overlay adds no Shannon information and can only change how the model uses its input (Shi et al., 2026); the two changes we saw are of that kind.

Wording, instructions and review.

“Do not miss any” wording, compared with a symmetric instruction not to miss or invent, has no measurable effect on SCP for any of the three models. Asking the model to localize each item relative to structures in the image has no significant effect, because current models have almost no location misses on these scenes. Same-view self-review, in which the model edits its own draft, confirms true and false records at nearly the same rate (h+≈h−h_{+}\approx h_{-}) and has no net gain on screen parsing; on FSC-147 it gave significant gains for 2 of 3 models, which we do not explain. Pairwise comparators that ask a model which of two reports is right judge whether something is an object rather than whether the box is precise, and are not used. Reasoning is not uniformly helpful: on 20 GroundCUA screens, GPT-6.1’s default setting raises set error by 18.7 per screen [5.8,34.3][5.8,34.3], through 16.3 additional false records and no fewer misses.

7.6 Detect errors: they persist, so ask someone else

Persistence.

Object-level errors repeat across calls. Intraclass correlations of reporting across repeated calls are 0.60 to 0.98 for true objects and 0.23 to 0.93 for false reports. On the detection sources, a binomial model with a common reporting probability is rejected in all 12 dataset and model cells, while a beta-binomial model fits. The share of misses that recur in every repeated call is 0.76 to 0.99 on the detection sources and 0.73 to 0.94 on the screen sources. In clicks, 64% to 83% of a model’s errors are repeated by a second call of the same model within the agreement tolerance.

A second model is a better alarm.

Persistence means that a second call of the same model rarely disagrees with the first where the first is wrong. A second model shares only part of the propensity. With the partner set by a fixed rule as the cheapest other model, the share of errors in which both calls agree on the same wrong point falls from 83% to 39% for GPT-6.1, from 64% to 29% for Sonnet 5.5, and from 73% to 48% for Gemini 3.8. In the risk-coverage analysis (Figure 6), at δ=1.5%\delta=1.5\%, the same-model alarm catches 17% of GPT-6.1’s errors (4 of 23) and the cross-model alarm catches 61% (14 of 23); for Sonnet 5.5 the shares are 36% and 71% (Table 12). The cross-model alarm sets more items aside, and Figure 6 shows the trade-off: where the two curves overlap, its miss rate at matched acceptance coverage is lower by 0.5 to 2.7 points (point estimates on 260 items, without intervals; for GPT-6.1 at 93.1% acceptance coverage it catches 9 of the 23 errors against 6 for the same-model alarm), and for GPT-6.1 and Sonnet 5.5 it reaches operating points with a miss rate of 3% to 4%, below the lowest same-model values (7.0% and 10.5%). After two-stage zoom the same pattern holds, so the advantage comes from the second model and not from zoom alone. We zoomed each model’s second click as well (772 calls), so that both alarms compare zoomed points. At δ=1.5%\delta=1.5\% a second zoomed call of the same model catches 40% to 50% of the remaining errors, and the partner’s zoomed point catches 68% to 78%, with miss rates of 2.6% to 3.6% on the 85% to 88% of items acted on (Table 12). The same-model alarm again acts on more items (93% to 94%); where the two curves overlap, the cross-model miss rate at matched acceptance coverage is lower by 0 to 1.5 points.

7.7 Repair a click by choosing among models

On the 260 click items of the GUI experiment, the GUI-grounding tier of Section 5.1 missed 11 targets against 16 for GPT-6.1’s two-stage zoom at its default setting. Table 13 reports it, with the baselines, on 600 further ScreenSpot-Pro items that share no item or screenshot with those 260. All 13,120 requests completed (13,126 attempts with retries; $44.93 at list prices for all arms), none of the fallbacks for a failed call, zoom, score or comparison was used, and every item stays in the denominator. Single-model flows sometimes returned no point, counted as a miss (Table 13); the three-model flows always returned one.

The tier against single-model practice.

On the 600 items the tier misses 56 targets (9.33%), against 82 (13.67%) for GPT-6.1’s two-stage zoom at its default setting: −4.33-4.33 points [−6.33,−2.33][-6.33,-2.33], with 34 items repaired and 8 broken (exact McNemar p=7×10−5p=7\times 10^{-5}). At about the same cost, three independent default zooms of GPT-6.1 with a cluster vote miss 76, so the tier’s miss rate is lower by 3.33 points (−3.33-3.33 [−5.17,−1.50][-5.17,-1.50], Holm-adjusted p=0.002p=0.002). Against a crop-first baseline that we implemented in the style of GUI-Lens (Fu et al., 2026), without its OCR and detector anchors or its verification step and with our own prompts, the tier misses 56 against 69: the difference is −2.17-2.17 points with an interval that reaches zero ([−4.17,0.00][-4.17,0.00]; Holm-adjusted p=0.060p=0.060), at 2.3 times that baseline’s cost.

Where the gain comes from.

Proposition 8 splits the tier’s 56 misses into 43 items on which no model’s zoomed point hits (FF), 3 on which a correct point exists but no cluster representative is correct (LL), and 10 on which the comparison picks the wrong representative (WW). With the scorer’s score alone, WW is 15 and the other two terms are unchanged. The comparison therefore repairs 8 items and breaks 3: its increment is −0.83-0.83 points [−2.00,0.17][-2.00,0.17], and −0.83-0.83 [−2.00,0.33][-2.00,0.33] with all three models at their lowest setting, neither significant. On the representative pairs in which exactly one point hits, a single comparison call names the right one in 85.9% of calls, and the two orders agree on 71 of 78 pairs, 64 of them correctly; on the 260 items of the GUI experiment the single-call rate was 88%. Against three GPT-6.1 zooms, most of the gain is in FF. One default zoom of GPT-6.1 has no correct point on 82 items; three of them, at about the tier’s cost, still have none on 62; the tier’s three models have none on 43. Proposition 9 names the rate behind this: on the 82 items that GPT-6.1 missed, a second GPT-6.1 zoom hits on 18% and a third, after two misses, on 7.5%, while Sonnet 5.5 hits on 29% and Gemini 3.8 on 37%, and Gemini 3.8 still hits on 26% of the 58 items that both GPT-6.1 and Sonnet 5.5 missed. On these items, repeating GPT-6.1 adds little coverage, consistent with its persistent errors (Section 7.6); the partners rescue more here, which Proposition 9 does not guarantee in general. The partners’ rates are close to those on the 260 click items of the GUI experiment, where one GPT-6.1 zoom has no correct point on 16 items: Sonnet 5.5 hits on 4 of them (25%), Gemini 3.8 on 6 (38%), and Gemini 3.8 on 3 of the 12 that both GPT-6.1 and Sonnet 5.5 missed (25%). Given the 82 items GPT-6.1 misses here, the rates from those items give 82×0.75×0.75≈4682\times 0.75\times 0.75\approx 46 items with no correct candidate among the 600, against 43 observed, although GPT-6.1 misses more than twice as often here (13.7% against 6.2%). Against the three-zoom vote, whose 76 misses are 62 items with no correct candidate and 14 later losses, 19 of the tier’s 20 fewer misses lie in candidate coverage.

Coverage needs selection.

A plain cluster vote over the same three models’ points, with no scorer (the largest cluster wins, ties go to the earliest source, whose point is returned), computed from the stored calls, misses 74 items (12.33%, $0.0205 per item), not significantly different from three GPT-6.1 zooms (−0.33-0.33 points [−1.83,1.17][-1.83,1.17]). It has the tier’s candidates, so its 74 misses are the same 43 items with no correct candidate and 31 later losses. Choosing by the scorer’s score and the comparison cuts those later losses to 13 (56 misses, 9.33%, $0.0273 per item): the tier’s miss rate is lower than the vote’s by 3.00 points (−3.00-3.00 [−4.67,−1.50][-4.67,-1.50]), with 22 items repaired and 4 broken (exact McNemar p=5×10−4p=5\times 10^{-4}). The other two models supply the candidates; the selection turns them into fewer misses.

Items without an alarm.

On 499 of the 600 items the three points form one cluster and no comparison is made. The tier misses 29 of them (5.8%), which is 52% of its misses. An action applied to all of them, or through a trigger independent of whether the base misses, improves accuracy only if rbrk<eT​rfix/(1−eT)r_{\mathrm{brk}}<e_{T}\,r_{\mathrm{fix}}/(1-e_{T}) with eT=5.8%e_{T}=5.8\% (Proposition 10): about 3.1% of the correct answers it touches if it repairs half of the misses. The scorer’s score alone misses 32 of the other 101 items (31.7%), which is where the comparison acts; the 260 click items of the GUI experiment show the same pattern (10 of 39 against 3 of 221). Nine clusters are chained, with two members farther apart than δ=1.5%\delta=1.5\%, and none is wider than 2.13% of the longer side.

Settings.

On the 600 items the default setting helps Sonnet 5.5 (misses −4.00-4.00 points [−6.17,−1.83][-6.17,-1.83] against its lowest setting) and does not change GPT-6.1 significantly (−0.67-0.67 [−2.67,1.33][-2.67,1.33]), the same direction as on the 260 items of the GUI experiment; the default setting also doubles the output cap (16,384 to 32,768 tokens).

The crop-first baseline errs elsewhere.

The crop-first baseline and the tier miss different items: both miss 42, only the baseline 27, only the tier 14. Of those 14, the baseline supplies a correct point on 7 items where all three of the tier’s models miss, so it is a new source in the sense of Proposition 9: added to the tier’s menu, it lowers the items with no correct candidate from 43 to 36 (ϕ=7/43\phi=7/43). On the other 7 the tier had a correct candidate and lost it (LL, 2 items) or chose wrongly (WW, 5). Conversely, on 14 of the 27 items that only the baseline misses, its wrong point lies within δ\delta of one of the tier’s candidates, so adding it to the vote would mostly strengthen wrong clusters (on 12 of the 14 every nearby candidate is wrong).

What a fourth source can add.

On the 57 items where the crop-first point and the tier’s point are more than δ\delta apart, the crop-first point is right and the tier’s wrong on 10, the reverse holds on 25, both are right on 12 and both wrong on 10. A rule that takes the crop-first point on aa of the first 10 items and on bb of the 25 changes the number of misses by b−ab-a, the count form of Proposition 10. Within this two-candidate, threshold-triggered menu the largest possible improvement is therefore 10 items (1.67 points). The comparison’s accuracy on the representative pairs above does not determine aa and bb on these different pairs, so we evaluated an enlarged candidate menu directly. We added the crop-first point as a fourth candidate, ranked last among sources, scored by the same scorer and handled by the same rules, on the same 600 items (717 further calls, $1.44). Items with no correct candidate fall from 43 to 36 (ϕ=7/43\phi=7/43). Lost representatives rise from 3 to 7 and wrong choices from 10 to 11. Of the 7 items where only the crop-first point is correct, the four-source tier gets 3 right; on 3 the point joins a cluster of wrong points and loses the representative choice to a wrong member with the same score, and on 1 the comparison picks a wrong representative. On the other items the added point repairs 1 and breaks 2: on one it displaces a correct representative, on the other the comparison turns to a wrong one. The four-source tier misses 54 items against 56 (−0.33-0.33 points [−1.17,0.34][-1.17,0.34]; 4 repaired, 2 broken) at $0.041 per item (12.5 calls) instead of $0.027. Proposition 8 accounts for the result term by term: the added source pays in FF and is charged in LL and WW. The tier of Algorithm 2 therefore stays at three sources, and the crop-first baseline is reported as a baseline.

7.8 Judge: selection has room left, but labels do not close it

Selection among a model’s own outputs.

Choosing the best feasible set from a model’s own three calls would remove 45.2% of set error relative to one call (median over 12 cells; Table 14), and 72% to 74% for GPT-6.1 on SKU-110K and DOTA. The constrained oracle differs from the unrestricted value on 25 of 720 images and has the same median. Record gates on output features, fitted with labels and evaluated by cross-fitting, reach 15.6% (logistic) and 14.6% (boosted trees); fitted on 10 labelled images they reach 13.2%. The more flexible selector does not help under cross-fitting, and its in-sample value (36.5%) is overfit. The empirical gap, median 26.1 points, combines information absent from the output features with selector and estimation shortfall (Proposition 7); our results bound it but do not apportion it. It measures the distance between the tested selectors and the best set in a fixed library of three calls, so it does not bound what adding calls or changing the library could gain. Within the operations we compared, the larger gains came from changing the information, a different view, model or readout, rather than from selecting among a model’s own outputs.

7.9 Judge: defaults that transfer

Table 15 (full values in Table B.4) evaluates construction transfer on stored reports: for each source, the construction that does best on the other five sources is applied to the stored calls of the sixth, so it is never chosen on the source it is evaluated on. Table 4 shows where the final defaults follow these transferred constructions and where they differ. For set error, the best same-model construction on the other five sources is three-call unanimity with averaged coordinates on every evaluated source. It lowers set error significantly in 9 of the 15 over-reporting cells and raises it significantly in none; on FSC-147, the under-reporting family, it is worse in 2 of 3 cells, consistent with Proposition 2 and Corollary 1. For F1, the transferred same-model construction is better in 2 cells, worse in 4 and not significant in 12, so the default is a single call. Three calls cost three times one call. From logged token usage at list prices, unanimity costs $0.029 to $0.21 per image for GPT-6.1 across the five over-reporting sources, $0.032 to $0.13 for Sonnet 5.5 and $0.011 to $0.058 for Gemini 3.8.

Configurations that transfer.

The same logic applies to the configuration of a single call: the reporting interface (one list for the whole image, or one row for each region of a fixed registry) and the reasoning setting. For each model, we chose among the four combinations on three detection sources and applied the choice to the fourth, so the labels of the evaluated source are used only to score it (Table 16). For F1, the chosen configuration is better than the list interface at the lowest setting in 5 of 12 cells and worse in 1 (Sonnet 5.5 on DocLayNet, −6.5-6.5 points); macro F1 rises from 42.1 to 49.1, against 51.7 for the best configuration of each cell chosen with its own labels, and the chosen calls cost 1.44 times as much. For set error, the same rule is better in 2 cells, worse in 1 and not significant in 9 (median change 0%), so the set-error defaults stay as in Table 4. One configuration shared by the three models transfers worse (F1: 5 cells better, 3 worse). The configuration that ships is chosen by the same rule on all four sources (GPT-6.1: regions, lowest; Sonnet 5.5: regions, default; Gemini 3.8: list, default; Table B.5).

When cross-model constructions are allowed, the transferred default improves set error in 12 of 18 cells and F1 in 10 of 18. It is better in 20 of the 24 cells in which the user’s model is not the strongest single model for that source and loss, and not significantly different in the other 4. All 5 cells in which it is significantly worse are cells where the user’s model is the strongest; for example, a three-model majority raises Sonnet 5.5’s set error on GroundCUA by 52% relative to one call, and a two-model intersection raises GPT-6.1’s on FSC-147 by 58%. Among constructions with averaged coordinates, against the best same-model construction chosen with all labels (a reference, not a deployable rule), the best cross-model construction is significantly better only on DOTA (−5.8%-5.8\%) and significantly worse on GroundCUA (+26.0%+26.0\%). When the user does not know which model is strongest, three-model unanimity is significantly better than three-call unanimity of a randomly chosen model on 4 of 5 over-reporting sources (−4%-4\% to −11%-11\%). Voting a strong model together with weaker ones is not a safe default: a three-model majority is 52% worse than GPT-6.1’s own three-call majority on FSC-147 and 59% worse than Sonnet 5.5’s on GroundCUA, an unzoomed three-model click vote on the 260 click items of the GUI experiment is 3.5 points below GPT-6.1 alone, and the per-type median of three models’ dense counts is 0.60 worse than Sonnet 5.5 alone. On aerial and shelf detection the same vote helps instead: it is 9.5% better than Sonnet 5.5’s three-call majority on DOTA and 4.7% better than Gemini 3.8’s on SKU-110K; on DocLayNet and ScreenParse it is not significantly different. Cross-model confirmation is therefore a menu option chosen with a few labels or a family-level ranking, while the cross-model alarm is a default whenever a second model is available.

8 Discussion

What a practitioner can take away.

Table 17 lists each component of the method with when to use it, its measured effect, where it does not help, and its cost; Table 4 gives the shipped settings and Appendix D the prompts. Three quantities decide most choices at run time: the degeneracy flags decide which count to read; agreement between two calls of one model measures stability, not correctness, so high agreement means another such call adds little; and the family default, or p1p_{1} estimated on a few labelled images, decides whether to delete unconfirmed records.

Why the gains come from changing information.

The theory and the measurements point the same way. Object-level persistence means that repeated calls of one model share most of their errors. In our comparisons, votes over the same outputs gained at most 23% for counts and 4.5% for clicks, and even a perfect selector over three calls can only choose among the records those calls contain. The largest gains we measured came from operations that change what is available: reading a different field of the same response, looking at a different view, or asking a model with a different model-specific component. Where those operations fail, the failures have the predicted form: deletion hurts when p1>1/2p_{1}>1/2, tiling can lose objects that no tile contains whole, and a partner hurts when its additional loss of true matches outweighs its additional rejection of false records, with the effect of averaged coordinates counted separately.

Where click accuracy can still come from.

Of the tier’s 56 remaining misses on the 600 click items, 43 have no correct candidate and 13 are lost in representation or choice (Proposition 8). A better rule over the same candidates can act only on the 13. The 43 need a source with a high rescue rate ϕ\phi on exactly those items, and its gain must survive representation and choice: of the crop-first source’s 7 rescues, 3 did (Section 7.7). On items where the models agree, any further action must meet the break-rate condition of Proposition 10. These two measurable quantities, the rescue rate on the items no candidate covers and the break rate on agreeing items, decide whether a further source or action raises accuracy, and both are measured from stored calls on labelled items.

What future models should change.

The measurements point to properties that model builders can target directly. A model’s stated summary should be computed from its own enumeration: GPT-6.1 and Sonnet 5.5 already list almost exactly the right number of objects, and their stated counts lose that information. Long lists should not degrade with position; Gemini 3.8 at its lowest setting drops class fields more often when consecutive records share a class; an order that interleaves classes lowers its count error and grouping by class raises it (Section 7.3). Class vocabularies given in the prompt should be respected, since Sonnet 5.5 still wrote “diamond” 258 times when the format named the allowed classes. Finally, errors that persist across calls limit what a fixed budget of resampling can repair; diversity across calls, or calibrated uncertainty at the object level, could make the cheaper same-model alarm as useful as a second model.

Scope of the results.

The theory’s guarantees hold under their stated conditions. The identities of Section 4.1 hold for any outputs and any fixed choice of maximum matching. Proposition 5 assumes deletion-only confirmation, no match takeover, and no ignore region or none of the base report’s false records inside one; outside these conditions the exact identity of Proposition 1 replaces it. The disagreement floor is a bound for point tasks and for boxes at IoU thresholds above 0.5; the click alarm is empirical and is evaluated by risk and acceptance coverage. Proposition 11 concerns model classes that admit scenes with identical or nearly identical output laws; when an object is reported with probability at most ϑ\vartheta per call, KK calls separate the two scenes by at most K​ϑK\vartheta in total variation. The readout repair applies where a readout gap exists: on our dense synthetic scenes the gap is most of the error, while on aerial and document images it is a small part of it for GPT-6.1 and Sonnet 5.5. Section 6 states how the reasoning setting and the output cap were separated. All results are for the model versions listed in Appendix C, at a total cost of about $758; we release every response and the analysis code, so the reported identities and tables can be reproduced without new model calls, while evaluating a new model version requires its own responses, analysed the same way.

Broader impact.

More accurate and auditable visual reports can make inventory, document and screen-automation systems more reliable, and an explicit status and alarm make failures visible instead of silent. The same techniques could make automated agents act with more confidence; our pipeline always returns a status and never claims certification without labels.

9 Conclusion

Reporting is part of the visual task, not merely its formatting. When vision-language models report sets of objects, part of their error is in the report rather than in the seeing. FSR treats reporting as a chain from responses to records, sets and readouts, which makes that error analysable. The chain gives exact identities for what each operation does, a behavioural model of persistent errors, and a proof that outputs alone cannot certify correctness when two scenes produce the same outputs. It also separates three problems. Repair works where the information is already present: read the count from the model’s list of records, not from the numbers it states, unless the list has degenerated; delete unconfirmed records only below the cost threshold; change the report structure, its decoding (declared aliases applied in code), the view or the model, rather than restating the same request more insistently. Error detection benefits most from a different source of evidence; on our click tasks a second model provided it better than a second call. For one click, the error splits exactly into missing candidates, lost representatives and wrong choices, which tells where to spend calls: FSR’s GUI-grounding tier, which adds two other models’ candidates and compares them only where they disagree, lowered the miss rate on 600 ScreenSpot-Pro items to 9.33%, against 13.67% for one model’s zoom and 12.33% for a plain vote over the same three models; against a crop-first baseline the difference was not significant. Judging between reports needs labels or a configuration transferred from other data; three-call unanimity, chosen on five sources, improved set error on most over-reporting cells of the sixth and did not significantly worsen it in any of them, while for F1 a single call remained the default, with an interface and setting per model on the detection sources. Every number in this paper can be regenerated from the released responses, with the DOTA, SKU-110K and FSC-147 labels rebuilt from their official downloads.

Appendix A Proofs and Supporting Results

Throughout, E⁡(S)=c⁡(S)+n−2​r​(S)E(S)=c(S)+n-2r(S) and Ew​(S)=cFP​[c⁡(S)−r⁡(S)]+cFN​[n−r⁡(S)]E_{w}(S)=c_{\mathrm{FP}}[c(S)-r(S)]+c_{\mathrm{FN}}[n-r(S)], with cc and rr computed from one fixed choice of maximum matching.

Lemma 1 (Matching size).

Fix the targets, a ground set of candidate records and the compatibility graph between them. Then S↦r⁡(S)S\mapsto r(S) is the rank function of a transversal matroid (Edmonds and Fulkerson, 1965): it never decreases when records are added, increases by 0 or 1 when one record is added, and is submodular (adding a record helps a smaller set at least as much as a larger one).

Proof of Lemma 1.

Consider the bipartite graph between records and targets with edges given by ρτ\rho_{\tau}. The subsets of records that can be matched simultaneously form the independent sets of a transversal matroid (Edmonds and Fulkerson, 1965), and the maximum matching size of SS is the rank of SS in that matroid. Matroid rank functions are monotone, satisfy r⁡(S∪{z})−r⁡(S)∈{0,1}r(S\cup\{z\})-r(S)\in\{0,1\}, and are submodular. ∎

Proposition 3.

The decomposition is a telescoping sum. Applying E=c+n−2​rE=c+n-2r to S0S_{0} and SfS_{f} gives the geometry term [c⁡(S0)−c⁡(Sf)]−2​[r⁡(S0)−r⁡(Sf)][c(S_{0})-c(S_{f})]-2[r(S_{0})-r(S_{f})]. Convexity of the squared distance gives ‖z¯−y‖2≤1m​∑i‖zi−y‖2\|\bar{z}-y\|^{2}\leq\frac{1}{m}\sum_{i}\|z_{i}-y\|^{2} for any target yy, so averaging does not increase mean squared error to any fixed target. A threshold matching is not monotone in squared error, however. If one member is within tolerance of yy and the other is far from every target, their mean can leave the tolerance ball of yy and a match is lost; conversely, two members just outside the tolerance on opposite sides of yy have a mean inside it, and a match is gained. Hence the geometry term can have either sign. ∎

Both errors are evaluated against the same nn for the same response, so their difference depends only on which field is read. Every rule g⁡(Φ)g(\Phi) takes values in 𝒮A\mathcal{S}_{A}, so pointwise ℓ⁡(g⁡(Φ),Y)≥minS∈𝒮A⁡ℓ⁡(S,Y)\ell(g(\Phi),Y)\geq\min_{S\in\mathcal{S}_{A}}\ell(S,Y); taking expectations and the infimum over gg gives Ror≤RΦ∗R_{\mathrm{or}}\leq R^{*}_{\Phi}. Proposition 12 (Constrained oracle).

For 𝒮A\mathcal{S}_{A} with at most one representative per cluster, including the option of choosing none, minS∈𝒮A⁡E⁡(S)=n−|M|\min_{S\in\mathcal{S}_{A}}E(S)=n-|M|, where MM is a maximum matching in the bipartite graph between clusters and targets that has an edge whenever some a∈A⁡(Q)a\in A(Q) is compatible with the target. It is attained by selecting one compatible representative for each matched cluster and nothing for the others.

Unrestricted matching over all records can exceed |M||M| when two members of one cluster match two targets; that value is not attainable within 𝒮A\mathcal{S}_{A} (Table 14 reports both).

Proof of Proposition 12.

Any S∈𝒮AS\in\mathcal{S}_{A} contains at most one record per cluster, so a maximum matching of SS to targets induces a cluster-target matching of size r⁡(S)r(S) in the stated graph; hence r⁡(S)≤|M|r(S)\leq|M|. Records unmatched in the chosen maximum matching and lying outside Ω\Omega add to cc, so c⁡(S)≥r⁡(S)c(S)\geq r(S) with or without ignore regions, and E⁡(S)=c⁡(S)+n−2​r​(S)≥n−r⁡(S)≥n−|M|E(S)=c(S)+n-2r(S)\geq n-r(S)\geq n-|M|. The construction that selects, for each cluster matched in MM, a representative compatible with its target, and nothing else, has r=c=|M|r=c=|M| and attains the bound. ∎

Proposition 8.

The output is a representative. If no candidate hits, the output misses (event of FF). Otherwise, if no representative hits, the output misses (event of LL). Otherwise some representative hits, and the output misses exactly in the event of WW. The three events are disjoint and their union is the event that the output misses.

Proposition 9.

Every candidate of the enlarged menu misses iff every earlier candidate misses and the added one misses, so the probability is F​Pr⁡(added misses∣all earlier miss)=F⁡(1−ϕ)F\,\Pr(\text{added misses}\mid\text{all earlier miss})=F(1-\phi) when F>0F>0, and 00 when F=0F=0. Under conditional independence given qq, Pr⁡(all miss∣q)=∏j=1k(1−qj)\Pr(\text{all miss}\mid q)=\prod_{j=1}^{k}(1-q_{j}); taking expectations gives FF.

Proposition 10.

The change in the miss indicator is 𝟙T​(𝟙​[b​ misses]−𝟙​[g​ misses])\mathbb{1}_{T}\,(\mathbb{1}[b\text{ misses}]-\mathbb{1}[g\text{ misses}]), which is +1+1 when bb misses and gg hits, −1-1 when bb hits and gg misses, and 00 otherwise. Its expectation is Pr⁡(T)​[Pr⁡(b​ misses,g​ hits∣T)−Pr⁡(b​ hits,g​ misses∣T)]=Pr⁡(T)​[eT​rfix−(1−eT)​rbrk]\Pr(T)[\Pr(b\text{ misses},g\text{ hits}\mid T)-\Pr(b\text{ hits},g\text{ misses}\mid T)]=\Pr(T)[e_{T}r_{\mathrm{fix}}-(1-e_{T})r_{\mathrm{brk}}]. If 𝟙T\mathbb{1}_{T} and 𝟙​[b​ misses]\mathbb{1}[b\text{ misses}] are independent given UU and T⊆UT\subseteq U, then Pr⁡(b​ misses∣T)=Pr⁡(b​ misses∣U,T)=Pr⁡(b​ misses∣U)\Pr(b\text{ misses}\mid T)=\Pr(b\text{ misses}\mid U,T)=\Pr(b\text{ misses}\mid U). The sample size for choosing a scorer follows from Hoeffding’s inequality for each scorer’s empirical miss rate with a union bound over the NsN_{\mathrm{s}} candidate scorers.

Proposition 11.

For any acceptance rule a⁡(H)∈[0,1]a(H)\in[0,1], the acceptance probability in world jj is ∫a​d​Pj\int a\,dP_{j}. If P0=P1P_{0}=P_{1} the two are equal, so acceptance at least 1−β1-\beta in world 0 forces acceptance at least 1−β>α1-\beta>\alpha in world 1 when α+β<1\alpha+\beta<1. In general, |∫a​d​P0−∫a​d​P1|≤TV⁡(P0,P1)|\int a\,dP_{0}-\int a\,dP_{1}|\leq\mathrm{TV}(P_{0},P_{1}) for 0≤a≤10\leq a\leq 1. For the hidden-target construction, couple the two worlds so that the output histories coincide unless the added target is reported in at least one of the KK calls, an event of probability at most K​ϑK\vartheta by the union bound, since the per-call bound ϑ\vartheta holds given the earlier history; non-interference means that, conditional on the target not being reported, the rest of the output has the same law in both worlds. The coupling inequality gives TV⁡(P0,P1)≤K​ϑ\mathrm{TV}(P_{0},P_{1})\leq K\vartheta. ∎

Corollary 1.

By assumption there is an admissible world in which the report over-counts, |S|>n0|S|>n_{0}. Add m>|S|−n0m>|S|-n_{0} targets that no interface reports and that do not change the rest of the output (ϑ=0\vartheta=0); by closure the result is admissible. The output law is unchanged and |S|<n0+m|S|<n_{0}+m, so the sign of the count gap differs between two worlds with the same output law. ∎

A.1 Explanatory parametrization and views

To describe how propensities vary with the model and the view when the rest of the interface is held fixed, that is, for calls that share the prompt, schema, setting and cap, we use the explanatory parametrization

logit​qo,η=ao+bo,m⁡(η)+γv⁡(η)​(o),\mathrm{logit}\,q_{o,\eta}=a_{o}+b_{o,m(\eta)}+\gamma_{v(\eta)}(o),
∑mbo,m=0,γv0​(o)=0,\textstyle\sum_{m}b_{o,m}=0,\qquad\gamma_{v_{0}}(o)=0,

where v0v_{0} is the whole image, aoa_{o} is common to all models (how hard the object is), bo,mb_{o,m} is specific to model mm, and γv​(o)\gamma_{v}(o) is the change from the whole image to view vv, which depends on the apparent size of oo in vv. All three terms may differ between prompts, schemas, settings and caps; a comparison that changes one of these compares two such parametrizations, not two terms of one. The form is related to item-response and labeler-expertise models, in which an item’s difficulty and a rater’s ability combine on the logit scale (Whitehill et al., 2009) (there as a product, here additively, as in Rasch-type models); here the items are objects and the raters are models and views. The two constraints are conventions that make the parts well defined: centering separates the shared part from the model-specific one, and the reference view separates both from the view effect. We do not estimate the parts; the parametrization motivates the predictions of Section 4.2, each of which is tested directly.

A view can raise how often objects are reported while the misses of the two calls stay as correlated, or become more so. For a true object drawn at random from the image, let AA and A′A^{\prime} indicate that two calls with the same interface report it and BB that a call on another view does, with means μA=μA′\mu_{A}=\mu_{A^{\prime}} and μB\mu_{B}, the calls being conditionally independent given the propensities. Then

P⁡(A=0,B=1)−P⁡(A=0,A′=1)\displaystyle P(A=0,B=1)-P(A=0,A^{\prime}=1)
=(1−μA)​(μB−μA)\displaystyle=(1-\mu_{A})(\mu_{B}-\mu_{A})
+Cov⁡(A,A′)−Cov⁡(A,B):\displaystyle+\mathrm{Cov}(A,A^{\prime})-\mathrm{Cov}(A,B):

the first term is the gain in how often objects are reported, the second the gain in complementarity. For example, with two equally likely kinds of object reported with probability 0.2 and 0.4 on the whole image, a view that adds log⁡2\log 2 to every logit gives 1/31/3 and 4/74/7: the mean rises from 0.30 to 0.45 and the covariance with the first call rises from 0.0100 to 0.0119, yet the probability that the first call misses an object and the second reports it is 0.305 for the new view against 0.200 for a repeated call: the gain in how often objects are reported (0.107) more than offsets a small loss of complementarity (0.002).

Appendix D Protocol Details

List-first prompt.

The full-protocol readout runs used the following system prompt for GPT-6.1 and Gemini 3.8 (native 0 to 1000 frame); the user message was “List every geometric shape in this image with its center, then counts by type. Respond with JSON only.”

You are a precise visual counting and localization assistant.

Given an image containing geometric shapes, identify every shape.
Report coordinates on a 0-1000 grid: x = 0 is the left edge and x = 1000 the
right edge of the image, y = 0 is the top edge and y = 1000 the bottom edge.
Use integers.
List the shapes in reading order: scan the image row by row from top to bottom,
and within a row from left to right.
The "type" value must be exactly one of: circle, triangle, square, star,
pentagon. A square rotated by any angle is still a "square"; do not use any
other type name.

Respond with ONLY a JSON object (no markdown, no commentary) in this format:
{"shapes": [{"type": "circle", "x": 402, "y": 311}, ...], "counts_by_type":
{"circle": 5, "triangle": 3, "square": 0, "star": 2, "pentagon": 4}}

Shape types to recognize: circle, triangle, square, star, pentagon.
Locate every shape carefully. Count systematically; do not miss any and do not
invent shapes that are not there.
Write the full shapes list first; after it, give counts_by_type for the shapes
you listed.

For Sonnet 5.5 the coordinate paragraph reads “The image is 1024x1024 pixels. Report coordinates as integer pixel positions in this image, where (0,0) is the top-left corner.” The count-first prompts of the readout experiment ask for counts_by_type before the list; all prompts are released with the responses.

Decoder.

The decoder strips a code fence and parses the whole response as JSON (L2). If that fails, it recovers each balanced {...} object that has the record fields (declared salvage) and reads counts_by_type if present, with its class names mapped by the same alias map (the pure-readout comparisons of Table 8 compare stated and list counts with neither mapped). Coordinates are mapped from the model’s frame to image pixels. Classes are lower-cased and mapped by the declared alias map; for SCP, {diamond, rhombus, rotated square} ↦\mapsto square. Records whose class is outside the vocabulary after mapping stay in the audit collection ZallZ^{\mathrm{all}}, are excluded from the delivered collection ZZ that set scores evaluate, and are counted by the first degeneracy flag; Table 10 adds a sensitivity that keeps them and scores them as unmatched. On the detection sources, records with a label outside the vocabulary or a box outside the image are likewise kept in the audit collection, excluded from delivery and counted as invalid (Table 2).

Degeneracy flags.

A list is flagged if any of the following holds: more than 10% of records lack a valid class; the list length is outside [0.5,1.5][0.5,1.5] times the stated total; more than 10% of records repeat a rounded coordinate pair already in the list; or the finish reason is “length”. The same thresholds are used for every model, including the open model.

Scoring and clustering.

Scoring uses the compatibility relation of each task in Table 2: for example, points of equal class within 30 pixels on SCP and 20 pixels on SCP-dense, detection boxes of equal class at IoU ≥0.75\geq 0.75, screen elements at IoU ≥0.5\geq 0.5 without class, and clicks inside the target box. Maximum matchings are computed with a linear assignment on the 0/1 compatibility matrix (Kuhn, 1955). Clusters across calls use the association rule of Table 2 (boxes: equal class and IoU ≥0.5\geq 0.5, also on the detection sources where scoring uses 0.75), with a maximum-cardinality, then maximum-overlap assignment against cluster representatives, and the averaged record is the coordinate mean of members.

Constructions.

Same-model: inter2 (two calls, intersection), union2, unan3 and maj3 (three calls, unanimity or majority), union3; each with averaged (_fus) or base-record (_del) coordinates. Cross-model: x2_inter and x2_union with a named partner, x3_unan and x3_maj over the three models (one call each), x3_union. The leave-one-source-out default for an evaluated source is the construction with the best mean relative change over the other five sources, computed separately for each loss and pool.

Alarms.

For clicks, the same-model alarm compares two unzoomed calls of one model; the cross-model alarm compares one unzoomed call of the user’s model with one of the partner; after zoom, the same-model alarm compares the model’s zoomed first click with its zoomed second click, and the cross-model alarm compares the zoomed first clicks of the two models. An item is set aside in the risk-coverage analysis when the two points are farther apart than δ\delta times the longer image side. The partner is set by a fixed rule, the cheapest other model per click call (GPT-6.1 and Sonnet 5.5: Gemini 3.8; Gemini 3.8: Sonnet 5.5).

Clicks from several models.

Candidates are the two-stage zoom points of Step 4, mapped to the original screenshot. A candidate’s identifier is the first 16 hexadecimal digits of the SHA-256 of the item, model, setting, parent call and coordinates. The scorer’s score request shows a native crop of one fifth of the screenshot’s width and height around the candidate, with a marker at the point, the instruction and the platform, and asks for a verdict and the probability that a click at the marker hits the intended element; it never names the model that produced the candidate. A missing or unreadable score counts as −1-1 for ranking. The comparison request shows the downscaled screenshot with both representatives marked by their identifiers and a native crop around each, asks which candidate satisfies the instruction (element, text, state, relation and whether the exact point lies inside the element), and allows “undecided”; it forbids proposing a new point. Each pair is sent in both orders, and the code asserts that the points drawn equal the representatives’ coordinates. Ranking keys, ties and failures follow Algorithm 2: a failed first click leaves that model without a candidate, a failed zoom keeps the first click, a failed comparison gives no win.

The 600 click items and baselines.

The 600 items were sampled from the ScreenSpot-Pro annotations not among the 200 ScreenSpot-Pro items of the GUI experiment, in proportion to each application file and, within it, to each pair of group and element type, with a fixed seed; they share no screenshot with those items. A first batch of 100 seeded items, part of the 600, was run through every arm to check costs and transport only; its calls are among the 13,126. The three-call baseline runs three independent default-setting zooms of GPT-6.1, clusters the three points with the same δ\delta, and returns the earliest point of the largest cluster (ties: the cluster with the earliest point). The crop-first baseline uses GPT-6.1 at its default setting: the first call must return a region of the downscaled screenshot, the second sees that region at native resolution with 8% padding and may return a smaller region or a click, and a third call, if needed, must click; an unreadable reply falls back to the centre of the last region. It follows the coarse-to-fine cropping of GUI-Lens (Fu et al., 2026) without its OCR and detector anchors or verification step, with our own prompts. Paired intervals resample screenshots (4,000 draws, seed 20261014); McNemar tests are exact.

Configuration transfer on the detection sources.

The menu contains the four single-call configurations run on every image of the four detection sources (first repetition): list or regions interface, each at the lowest and the default setting. In the regions interface the model returns one row per region of a fixed coordinate registry, with a status of empty, found or unknown, and reports each object in the region that contains its centre; in the list interface it returns one list for the whole image in registry scan order. For each model and evaluated source, F1 picks the configuration with the highest mean of per-source mean F1 on the other three sources, and set error the one with the lowest mean relative change against the list interface at the lowest setting; ties keep the earlier configuration in the order list-lowest, regions-lowest, list-default, regions-default. Intervals are paired bootstrap intervals over the images of the evaluated source.

Prompts below are verbatim; line breaks inside long lines are added for display. Reproducing the tables.

The code and all requests and responses are at https://github.com/shijunzhe/vlm-set-reporting, together with the labels whose licences allow redistribution (DocLayNet, ScreenSpot-Pro, ScreenSpot-v2, GroundCUA, ScreenParse, PixMo-Count). The labels of DOTA v1.0, SKU-110K and FSC-147 are not redistributed: the repository stores a placeholder for each value, naming the official file and the window, scale and rounding applied, and thirdparty/tp.py rebuilds the files from the official downloads, writing a file only when its SHA-256 digest matches the file we scored against. bash reproduce.sh --sources <dir> performs this rebuild, sets the paths, runs stageB/analysis/run_all.sh, which recomputes the data of every table and figure in Section 7, and writes the LaTeX tables and figures; without --sources it recomputes the analyses that do not score against those three label sets and keeps the shipped outputs of the others. No step calls a model. The synthetic dense images are regenerated, byte for byte, with

python3 -I stageB/code/scp_generate.py --num_images 50 --min_shapes 120 \
        --max_shapes 200 --min_radius 9 --max_radius 16 --seed 2026
